name: Dawn of agriculture
summary: Farming was developed independently in several regions, beginning with the Fertile Crescent, and permanently changed how humans live.
body:
Agriculture is the deliberate cultivation of plants and herding of animals. It was taken up independently in at least eleven regions of the world between roughly 10,000 and 4,000 BCE, the earliest and best documented beginning being in the Fertile Crescent, the arc of hill country running from the Levant through southern Anatolia to the Zagros. The shift from foraging to farming is usually called the Neolithic Revolution, although it took thousands of years.

Eight founder crops were domesticated in the Fertile Crescent: emmer and einkorn wheat, barley, lentil, pea, chickpea, bitter vetch and flax. Sheep, goats, pigs and cattle followed. Elsewhere the same shift began from different material: rice and millet in China, maize, beans and squash in Mesoamerica, potatoes and quinoa in the Andes, sorghum and yams in Africa, taro and banana in New Guinea.

Farming produced storable surpluses, and surpluses supported permanent villages, property, craft specialisation, hierarchy, and eventually cities and states. It also fed far more people from the same ground: world population, small and slow-growing throughout the Palaeolithic, began a rise that has not stopped.

The costs are visible in the skeletons. Early farmers were shorter than the foragers before them, had worse teeth and more signs of nutritional stress, and worked longer hours on a narrower diet. Living beside dense herds also gave humans measles, smallpox, influenza and tuberculosis.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic_Revolution).

steps.name: The founder crops of the Fertile Crescent
steps.page: Wild stands of emmer and einkorn wheat, barley and pulses were harvested in the Levant and upper Mesopotamia long before they were sown. Over roughly a millennium the harvested populations changed: seed heads stopped shattering, grains grew larger, and the plants became dependent on people to sow them. This is the domestication of the eight founder crops, the best documented of the early origins of farming.

steps.name: Rice farming in the Yangtze valley
steps.page: Rice was domesticated from wild stands in the middle and lower Yangtze; millet was domesticated separately on the drier loess soils of the Yellow River basin. The two are the agricultural foundation of Chinese civilisation, and both were domesticated independently of the Fertile Crescent.

steps.name: Maize domesticated in Mexico
steps.page: Maize was bred out of teosinte, a grass whose ear is a fraction of the size, in the Balsas river valley of southern Mexico. Combined later with beans and squash, it became the staple of every Mesoamerican and, eventually, of much of North America and the Andes.

steps.name: Farming reaches Europe
steps.page: Farmers moved from Anatolia into Greece and the Balkans, then up the Danube and along the Mediterranean coast, carrying the Fertile Crescent crop package with them. Ancient DNA shows this was largely a migration of people rather than the spread of an idea: European farmers descend substantially from Anatolian ancestors, mixed to varying degrees with the hunter-gatherers already there.

name: Göbekli Tepe
summary: Hunter-gatherers raised monumental carved pillars in southeastern Anatolia, before pottery or farming villages.
body:
Part of [Dawn of agriculture](event:agriculture). Göbekli Tepe is a hilltop site in south-eastern Anatolia where hunter-gatherers raised circles of monumental carved pillars from about 9500 BCE, before pottery, metal, the wheel or farming villages. It is among the oldest known monumental architecture anywhere.

The enclosures are rings of T-shaped limestone pillars, the largest about 5.5 m tall and weighing several tonnes, set into a low wall with two taller pillars in the centre. Many are carved in relief with foxes, boars, snakes, scorpions, cranes and vultures, and some carry arms and hands that make the T-shape read as a stylised human figure. The stone was quarried on the same plateau, where unfinished pillars still lie.

Excavation began in 1995 under Klaus Schmidt. He argued the site was a sanctuary rather than a settlement, built by people who still lived by hunting and gathering, which would mean that large-scale ritual gathering preceded settled [farming](event:agriculture) rather than following it. Later work has complicated that reading: there is evidence of domestic buildings, water cisterns and long-term occupation, so the sharp division between temple and village is no longer secure. The enclosures were deliberately backfilled, which is why they survive. The site was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2018 and remains largely unexcavated.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Göbekli_Tepe).

name: Walls of Jericho
summary: One of the world's oldest continuously occupied settlements built a stone wall and tower.
body:
Part of [Dawn of agriculture](event:agriculture). Jericho, in the Jordan valley near a perennial spring, is one of the oldest continuously occupied places on Earth. Around 8000 BCE its inhabitants built a stone wall around the settlement and a stone tower some 8.5 m high inside it, the earliest known monumental construction of their kind.

The site was occupied from about 9600 BCE, first as a village of round mud-brick houses covering a few hectares and holding perhaps several hundred people. The wall and tower belong to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A phase. They were long read as defences, but flood protection and communal display have both been argued for instead; nothing about the site indicates a war. Later inhabitants plastered and painted over human skulls, setting shells in the eye sockets, a burial practice found across the Neolithic Levant.

Kathleen Kenyon's excavations in the 1950s established the sequence and the radiocarbon dates. They also showed that the walls of the biblical siege story do not match the archaeology: the Bronze Age city on the mound was already in decline or abandoned at the period usually proposed for it. Occupation of the tell continued, with breaks, into the Iron Age, and the modern town lies beside it.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jericho).

name: Domestication of livestock
summary: Sheep, goats, pigs and cattle were brought under human management, followed later by the horse.
body:
Part of [Dawn of agriculture](event:agriculture). Between roughly 8500 and 3500 BCE the animals that agriculture depended on were brought under human management: sheep and goats first, then pigs and cattle, and later the donkey, the horse and the camel. The dog had already been domesticated from the wolf thousands of years earlier, by hunters.

Sheep and goats were taken from wild populations in the Zagros and eastern Anatolia; cattle descend from the aurochs, domesticated separately in the Near East and in South Asia; pigs from wild boar in more than one place. Managed herds gave meat that could be stored on the hoof, and then a series of products that a killed animal cannot give repeatedly: milk, wool, dung for fuel and fertiliser, and traction. Ploughing and cartage roughly multiplied the area one household could work. Adult lactose tolerance spread through several herding populations as a consequence of the milk.

Living close to dense herds also moved diseases across the species barrier. Measles, smallpox, influenza and tuberculosis all have animal reservoirs, and the epidemic diseases of the farming world are largely inherited from its livestock. The horse, domesticated on the Eurasian steppe in the fourth millennium BCE and later harnessed to the [wheel](event:wheel), changed warfare and long-distance travel more than any other animal.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestication_of_animals).

name: Çatalhöyük
summary: A dense Neolithic town in Anatolia housing several thousand people in mudbrick houses entered through the roof.
body:
Part of [Dawn of agriculture](event:agriculture). Çatalhöyük was a large Neolithic settlement on the Konya plain of southern Anatolia, occupied from about 7100 to 5700 BCE. At its height several thousand people lived there, which makes it one of the largest known settlements of its age.

The town had no streets. Mud-brick houses were packed wall to wall and entered through a hole in the flat roof, reached by ladder; the roofs served as the circulation space. Houses were rebuilt on the footprint of their predecessors, so the mound rose about 20 m over some 1,500 years. Interiors were plastered and regularly replastered, and many carry wall paintings, bulls' horns set into benches and pillars, and modelled reliefs. The dead were buried beneath the floors of the houses they had lived in.

Nothing at the site has been identified as a palace, temple or administrative building, and the houses differ little in size or contents, which is why Çatalhöyük is regularly cited in arguments about how early and how inevitably social hierarchy followed [farming](event:agriculture). Its people grew wheat and barley, herded sheep and goats, and still hunted. James Mellaart excavated in the 1960s and Ian Hodder from 1993; the site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Çatalhöyük).

name: Rise of Uruk and the first cities
summary: Uruk in southern Mesopotamia grew into what is often called the world's first city, with tens of thousands of inhabitants.
body:
Uruk, in southern Mesopotamia on a former channel of the Euphrates, grew during the fourth millennium BCE into what is often called the world's first city. At its height it may have held 40,000 people inside its walls and as many again in the surrounding countryside.

The city was built around two monumental precincts, Eanna and Kullaba, dedicated to Inanna and to An. Their temple platforms, terraces and cone-mosaic facades required labour on a scale no village could raise. Around them the characteristic marks of a state-scale society appear together: mass-produced bevelled-rim bowls turned out in the thousands, presumably as ration containers; cylinder seals used to mark ownership and authorise transactions; and the beginnings of a bureaucracy to track both.

The accounting needs of that bureaucracy produced the first [writing](event:writing), clay tablets of pictographic signs recording quantities of grain, beer, livestock and labour, which over the following centuries developed into cuneiform. The 'Uruk expansion' carried the city's material culture up the Euphrates and into Iran, whether by colony, trade or emulation. Uruk was later remembered as the city of Gilgamesh, and it remained inhabited into the first millennium CE.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruk).

name: Invention of the wheel
summary: Potters' wheels and then wheeled vehicles appeared across Mesopotamia and the Pontic steppe.
body:
The wheel appears in the archaeological record of the fourth millennium BCE, first as the potter's wheel and then, within a few centuries, as the wheel of a vehicle. The earliest evidence for wheeled transport comes from Mesopotamia, the Northern Caucasus and Central Europe at close to the same time, and it is not settled which came first.

The difficulty lay in the axle rather than the disc. A wheel is only useful with an axle, and the axle has to be exactly perpendicular to the wheel and fitted closely enough not to wobble but loosely enough to turn, a problem in precision woodworking rather than in insight, which is why the invention arrives long after the drill, the loom and agriculture. Early vehicles used a fixed axle turning with the wheels, or wheels turning on a fixed axle; both are found.

The evidence is a pictograph of a wagon on a tablet from Uruk (about 3400 BCE), a wagon painted on a pot from Bronocice in Poland, model wagons from the steppe and surviving wooden wheels from Slovenia and Switzerland. Wagons drawn by oxen moved bulk goods overland for the first time; the light spoked wheel, developed around 2000 BCE, made the war chariot possible. Wheels were never adopted for transport in the pre-Columbian Americas, where wheeled toys are known but draught animals were not.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheel).

name: Bronze Age begins
summary: Alloying copper with tin produced a metal hard enough for tools and weapons, and trade networks to carry the ingredients.
body:
The Bronze Age is the period in which bronze (copper alloyed with tin, and sometimes arsenic) became the principal material for tools, weapons and prestige goods. It began in the Near East around 3300 BCE and ended there with the [Late Bronze Age collapse](event:bronze-age-collapse) shortly after 1200 BCE, though the dates differ region by region.

Bronze is harder than copper, casts well and can be sharpened and recast, which made it worth the trouble it took to obtain. That trouble was considerable: tin is rare and is almost never found beside copper, so bronze could only be made by societies plugged into long-distance exchange. Tin reached the Mediterranean from Afghanistan, from Anatolia and from Cornwall; copper came from Cyprus, Oman and the Alps. The Uluburun shipwreck, sunk off Anatolia in the fourteenth century BCE, was carrying ten tonnes of Cypriot copper and a tonne of tin.

The metal is therefore inseparable from the palace economies that organised its supply: Egypt, the Hittites, Assyria, Babylon, the Mycenaeans and the Minoans, linked by diplomacy, tribute and trade. That dependence on distant supply was also a fragility. When the network broke in the twelfth century BCE, the states that ran on it broke too, and [iron](event:iron-age), whose ore is common almost everywhere, replaced bronze for working edges.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age).

name: Invention of writing
summary: Cuneiform accounting marks in Sumer became the first true writing system, with Egyptian hieroglyphs following within a century or two.
body:
Writing is the recording of language in visible signs. It was invented independently at least three and probably four times: in Sumer around 3200 BCE, in Egypt at almost the same date, in China by about 1200 BCE, and in Mesoamerica by about 500 BCE. The Sumerian system is the earliest for which the development can be followed step by step.

It began as accounting. Clay tokens representing quantities of grain, oil and livestock were sealed in clay envelopes, then impressed on the outside of them, then drawn on flat tablets as pictographs, a running record of what the temples of [Uruk](event:uruk) had received and paid out. Signs were pressed into damp clay with a reed stylus, which turned curved pictures into wedge-shaped strokes: cuneiform. The decisive move was phonetic. Once a sign could stand for the sound of a word rather than the thing, names, verbs and grammar could be written, and the system could record anything the language could say.

Egyptian hieroglyphs appear within a century or two, complete enough that borrowing of the idea is likely even though the signs are unrelated. Chinese writing is first attested on Shang [oracle bones](event:oracle-bones); Maya and Zapotec scripts arose with no contact with the Old World at all. All of them came to be used for law, contracts, literature and mathematics, and they leave records that historians can read directly rather than infer.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_writing).

name: Unification of Egypt
summary: Upper and Lower Egypt were unified under a single king, traditionally Narmer, beginning three millennia of pharaonic civilisation.
body:
Around 3100 BCE Upper and Lower Egypt (the Nile valley and the Delta) were brought under a single king, beginning the Early Dynastic Period and roughly three thousand years of pharaonic rule. Tradition names the first king Menes; he is usually identified with Narmer, and possibly with his successor Hor-Aha.

The unification is attested less by a narrative than by objects. The Narmer Palette, a ceremonial siltstone plaque from Hierakonpolis, shows the king wearing the white crown of Upper Egypt on one face and the red crown of Lower Egypt on the other, striking down a captive. Whether it records a single conquest or commemorates a process already long under way is disputed; the material culture of Upper Egypt had been spreading north for generations.

What emerged was a centralised state: a divine kingship, a capital at Memphis at the junction of the two lands, a system of nomes administered by royal officials, a national grain tax based on the Nile flood, and hieroglyphic writing to record it. Royal tombs at Abydos and later the pyramid field at Saqqara mark its wealth. The state survived three later periods of collapse and reunification.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Dynastic_Period_(Egypt)).

name: Minoan civilization of Crete
summary: A seafaring Bronze Age culture on Crete built palaces, a merchant fleet and an undeciphered script.
body:
The Minoan civilization was a Bronze Age culture centred on Crete, flourishing from about 2700 to 1450 BCE. It was named by Arthur Evans, who excavated Knossos from 1900, after the legendary king Minos. It is often described as the first civilization in Europe.

Its most conspicuous remains are the palace complexes at Knossos, Phaistos, Malia and Zakros, multi-storey complexes of courts, workshops, light wells and storerooms, with drainage and plumbing, brightly painted frescoes of bulls, dolphins and processions, and magazines holding hundreds of large storage jars. They appear to have been administrative and redistributive centres as much as royal residences. The Minoans were seafarers and traders, in contact with Egypt, the Levant and the Aegean islands, and their towns are largely unfortified.

They wrote in Cretan hieroglyphs and then in Linear A, which can be sounded out through its later Mycenaean adaptation but records a language still unidentified. The [eruption of Thera](event:thera-eruption) devastated the southern Aegean in the seventeenth or sixteenth century BCE; its role in the culture's decline is argued over. By about 1450 BCE most Cretan sites had been destroyed and Knossos was being administered in Greek, in Linear B, by [Mycenaeans](event:mycenaean-greece).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_civilization).

name: Indus Valley civilisation
summary: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa held grid-planned cities with drains, standardised bricks and a script still undeciphered.
body:
The Indus Valley Civilisation flourished from about 2600 to 1900 BCE across what is now Pakistan and north-western India, the basins of the Indus and the seasonal Ghaggar-Hakra. It was the largest of the three early Old World civilisations by area, covering more ground than Egypt and Mesopotamia together, and was unknown until excavations at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro in the 1920s.

The civilisation is noted for its cities. Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were laid out on a grid, built of standardised kiln-fired bricks in fixed proportions, and provided with covered drains, wells and bathing platforms, among the earliest urban sanitation systems known. Weights follow a single binary-decimal standard from one end of the civilisation to the other. Seals carved with animals and short inscriptions turn up as far away as Mesopotamia, where the trading partner was known as Meluhha.

No palaces, royal tombs, temples or clear military installations have been identified, and no ruler has been named, so the political organisation is not understood. The Indus script, known from thousands of short inscriptions, is undeciphered, and it is not agreed that it records a language at all. From about 1900 BCE the cities were gradually abandoned as the population shifted east, probably as monsoon rainfall weakened and river courses changed.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_Valley_Civilisation).

name: Stonehenge
summary: The sarsen circle was raised on Salisbury Plain, aligned on the solstice sunrise and sunset.
body:
Stonehenge is a prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, England. The ring of standing sarsen stones capped with lintels, the form the site is known by, was raised between about 2600 and 2400 BCE, at the end of the Neolithic.

Construction ran over some 1,500 years in phases. It began around 3000 BCE as a circular earthwork bank and ditch with a ring of pits, used for cremation burials. The bluestones (up to four tonnes each, brought some 250 km from the Preseli hills of west Wales) were set up next. Then came the sarsens: local sandstone blocks of about 25 tonnes, dressed and joined with mortice-and-tenon and tongue-and-groove joints borrowed from carpentry, arranged as an outer circle and an inner horseshoe of five trilithons.

The monument is aligned on the solstices: the axis runs towards sunrise at the summer solstice in one direction and sunset at the winter solstice in the other. Around it lie hundreds of burial mounds and, 3 km away, the timber circles and settlement of Durrington Walls, where feasting debris suggests people gathered from across Britain. Its purpose is not recorded; a burial ground, a ceremonial centre and a solar calendar have all been argued. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1986.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonehenge).

name: Great Pyramid of Giza
summary: Khufu's tomb, 146 metres tall and built from over two million blocks, was the tallest structure on Earth for 3,800 years.
body:
Part of [Unification of Egypt](event:egypt-unification). The Great Pyramid of Giza was built as the tomb of the Fourth Dynasty pharaoh Khufu, around 2560 BCE, over an estimated twenty years. At 146.6 m it was the tallest structure made by human beings for some 3,800 years, and it is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing.

It contains roughly 2.3 million blocks of limestone and granite, most of them quarried on the plateau itself, with the fine casing limestone brought from Tura across the river and the granite of the burial chamber from Aswan, 800 km upstream. The base is level to within a few centimetres and the sides are aligned on the cardinal directions to a fraction of a degree. Inside are three chambers, a corbelled Grand Gallery and a set of narrow shafts whose function is still argued.

The workers' town excavated south-east of the pyramid, with bakeries, breweries and cattle bones, together with papyri from Wadi al-Jarf recording a gang delivering casing stone, indicate a paid and organised workforce housed and fed by the state rather than the mass of slaves of later legend. How the blocks were raised is not recorded; ramps of several geometries have been proposed and none is proven. The casing was stripped in the medieval period, leaving the stepped core visible today.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza).

name: Akkadian Empire
summary: Sargon of Akkad conquered the Sumerian cities and assembled what is often called the first empire.
body:
The Akkadian Empire was founded by Sargon of Akkad in the twenty-fourth century BCE, when he conquered the Sumerian city-states of southern Mesopotamia and the lands around them. It is frequently called the first empire in history: the first state to rule several previously independent peoples from one centre for an extended period.

Sargon's inscriptions claim campaigns from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean. He installed Akkadian-speaking governors in conquered cities, put his daughter Enheduanna, the earliest author known by name, in charge of the moon god's temple at Ur, and kept a standing force said to number 5,400 men who 'ate bread daily before him'. Akkadian, a Semitic language, became the administrative tongue alongside Sumerian and stayed the lingua franca of the Near East for well over a millennium. His grandson Naram-Sin extended the conquests and had himself written as a god.

The capital, Akkad, has never been located. The empire fell apart after about 180 years, and later Mesopotamian tradition blamed the Gutians from the Zagros. Sediment cores and other palaeoclimate evidence have been used to argue that a severe, centuries-long drought beginning around 2200 BCE was the underlying cause; the case is contested but widely discussed. Ur then revived under the [Third Dynasty](event:ur-nammu-code).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akkadian_Empire).

name: Code of Ur-Nammu
summary: The oldest surviving law code predates Hammurabi by about three centuries, setting out written justice in Sumer.
body:
The Code of Ur-Nammu is the oldest surviving law code, written in Sumerian around 2100 BCE, roughly three centuries before the [Code of Hammurabi](event:hammurabi). It is attributed either to Ur-Nammu, founder of the Third Dynasty of Ur, or to his son Shulgi.

It survives only in later clay-tablet copies, the first identified in 1952 from a fragment in Istanbul, and is incomplete: a prologue and about thirty of an estimated forty or more laws can be read. The prologue has the king claim that the gods appointed him, and that he established equity in the land, protecting the orphan and the widow and stopping the powerful from seizing the property of the weak.

The laws themselves are conditional: 'if a man does X, then Y'. They cover homicide, robbery, false accusation, adultery, injury, runaway slaves, negligent flooding of a neighbour's field, and the obligations of marriage and divorce. For bodily injury they set monetary compensation in silver (a broken bone or a severed foot is paid for by weight), where Hammurabi's later code would in some cases prescribe retaliation in kind. Whether the code was applied in court or was a statement of royal justice for display is debated, but it shows written law already established in Mesopotamia at the end of the third millennium BCE.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_of_Ur-Nammu).

name: Egypt's Middle Kingdom
summary: Egypt was reunited after the First Intermediate Period, in what is conventionally treated as a classical age of Egyptian art and literature.
body:
The Middle Kingdom is the period of Egyptian history running from about 2055 to 1650 BCE, from the reunification of the country by Mentuhotep II of Thebes after the First Intermediate Period to the fragmentation that let the Hyksos take the Delta. It is conventionally treated as a classical age of Egyptian art, literature and administration.

Mentuhotep II ended more than a century of division between rival dynasties at Herakleopolis and Thebes. The Twelfth Dynasty that followed moved the capital north to Itjtawy near the Faiyum, where Amenemhat III's irrigation and land reclamation works brought a large new area under cultivation. Egyptian control was pushed south into Nubia behind a chain of massive mud-brick fortresses at the second cataract, and trade ran to Punt, Byblos and the Aegean.

The literature of the period (the Tale of Sinuhe, the Eloquent Peasant, the Instruction of Amenemhat) was copied as a model of style for the next thousand years, and its language became the classical form of written Egyptian. Royal sculpture turned from the serene idealism of the Old Kingdom to careworn, individual faces. Pyramids were still built, but of mud brick with stone casing, and most have collapsed. Central authority weakened through the Thirteenth Dynasty until the kingdom broke apart again.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Kingdom_of_Egypt).

name: Code of Hammurabi
summary: The Babylonian king had 282 laws carved on a basalt stele and set up in public.
body:
The Code of Hammurabi is a Babylonian legal text of about 1755–1750 BCE, inscribed on a black basalt stele more than two metres high and set up in public. It is not the earliest law code (the [Code of Ur-Nammu](event:ur-nammu-code) is three centuries older), but it is by far the longest and most complete to survive from the ancient Near East.

The stele carries a relief of Hammurabi standing before Shamash, god of justice, and then some 282 laws in cuneiform, framed by a prologue and an epilogue in which the king states that he was raised up to make justice prevail and to stop the strong oppressing the weak. The laws are casuistic (each states a case and its ruling) and cover contract, wages, property, debt, family, inheritance, slavery, medicine, building and agriculture.

Penalties depend on the status of the parties. Between men of equal rank the code applies retaliation in kind, the principle later summarised as an eye for an eye; injuries to a commoner or a slave are compensated in silver instead. Some provisions prescribe death or mutilation, others set compensation, and a number presume the accused innocent until the accuser proves the charge. The stele was carried off to Susa as plunder in the twelfth century BCE and excavated there in 1901; it is now in the Louvre.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_of_Hammurabi).

name: Rise of the Hittite Empire
summary: The Hittites of Anatolia built an empire that rivalled Egypt and fought Ramesses II to a standstill at Kadesh.
body:
The Hittites were an Anatolian people who built one of the great powers of the Late Bronze Age, ruling from Hattusa in the bend of the Halys river from about 1650 to 1180 BCE. At its height the empire reached across Anatolia and into northern Syria, where it met Egypt.

Its state was a network of vassal kingdoms bound by treaty to the Great King rather than a uniformly administered territory, and the treaties, letters and law codes recovered from the Hattusa archives are the best documentation of Bronze Age diplomacy that exists. The law code prescribes capital punishment less often than its Mesopotamian counterparts, preferring restitution. The Hittites wrote in cuneiform, in an Indo-European language, the earliest attested, alongside Luwian hieroglyphs.

Their army was built around the chariot, and they fought Ramesses II at [Kadesh](event:kadesh) around 1274 BCE. Neither side won; the treaty concluded sixteen years later survives in both Egyptian and Hittite versions and is the earliest international peace agreement whose text is known. The Hittites were long credited with the invention of iron smelting, a claim now much qualified, though they did work iron for prestige objects. Hattusa was burned and abandoned in the [Late Bronze Age collapse](event:bronze-age-collapse); smaller Syro-Hittite states carried the name on for several more centuries.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hittites).

name: Eruption of Thera
summary: One of the largest eruptions of the Holocene destroyed the Minoan town of Akrotiri on Santorini.
body:
The Minoan eruption of Thera (the volcano of Santorini, in the southern Aegean) was one of the largest volcanic events of the last ten thousand years. It ejected on the order of 60 cubic kilometres of material, blew out the centre of the island and left the caldera that the surviving crescent of Thera encloses today.

Its date is one of the long-running disputes of Aegean archaeology. Radiocarbon and the tree-ring record put it in the seventeenth century BCE, around 1600 BCE or a little earlier; the conventional Egyptian pottery chronology puts it more than a century later, in the sixteenth. The two have not been fully reconciled.

The Bronze Age town of Akrotiri on the island was buried under metres of pumice and ash. Like Pompeii, it is preserved in exceptional detail (multi-storey houses, drainage, stored goods, and wall paintings of ships, antelopes and boxing boys), but unlike Pompeii it holds no bodies and little jewellery, so its people appear to have left in time. Ashfall and tsunamis struck northern Crete and the surrounding coasts. Whether the eruption caused the decline of [Minoan Crete](event:minoan-civilization), which continued for well over a century afterwards, is doubted; the connection to the legend of Atlantis is speculation.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_eruption).

name: Mycenaean civilization
summary: Mainland Greek palace kingdoms built citadels, traded across the Mediterranean and left the first written Greek.
body:
Mycenaean Greece was the last phase of the Bronze Age on the Greek mainland, running from about 1600 to 1100 BCE. It was the first advanced civilisation in mainland Greece, organised around fortified palace centres at Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos, Thebes and elsewhere, and it takes its name from the richest of them.

The palaces were run by a ruler titled *wanax* and a warrior aristocracy, and they administered their territories closely: the Linear B tablets baked hard in the fires that destroyed the archives record rations, land holdings, textile production, chariot parts and offerings to gods including Zeus, Hera and Poseidon. Linear B was deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952 and proved to be an early form of Greek, adapted from Minoan Linear A, which pushed the history of the Greek language back some five centuries.

Mycenaean citadels were built of cyclopean masonry, blocks so large that later Greeks thought giants had laid them, and their elite were buried in shaft graves and then in corbelled tholos tombs with gold masks and inlaid weapons. They traded across the Mediterranean, took over [Crete](event:minoan-civilization) around 1450 BCE, and are widely identified with the Ahhiyawa of Hittite letters. The palaces were destroyed in the [Late Bronze Age collapse](event:bronze-age-collapse); writing was lost, and later Greeks remembered the age only through legend such as the [Trojan War](event:trojan-war).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_Greece).

name: Shang dynasty
summary: The first Chinese dynasty attested by contemporary writing, ruling from Anyang with bronze ritual vessels and oracle bones.
body:
The Shang was the second of the traditional Chinese dynasties and the first for which contemporary written evidence exists. It ruled the middle and lower Yellow River valley from about 1600 to 1046 BCE, the later part of the period from a capital at Yin, near modern Anyang.

Excavation at Anyang from 1928 turned a dynasty known only from later histories into a documented one. Its royal tombs held bronze ritual vessels, jade, chariots, and the remains of sacrificed humans and animals; the tomb of the consort and general Fu Hao, found intact in 1976, contained more than 400 bronzes and 700 jades. Shang bronze casting, using ceramic piece-moulds rather than lost wax, was among the most technically advanced of its time.

The [oracle bones](event:oracle-bones), ox shoulder blades and turtle plastrons inscribed with divinations put to the royal ancestors, carry the earliest known Chinese writing, already a mature system ancestral to the script in use today. They record questions about harvests, childbirth, illness, weather, hunting and war, and they preserve a king list that matches the received tradition closely. The last Shang king was overthrown by the [Zhou](event:zhou-dynasty) at the battle of Muye.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shang_dynasty).

name: Vedic period in India
summary: The Vedas were composed in Sanskrit, laying the foundations of Hindu religion, ritual and social order.
body:
The Vedic period is the era in northern Indian history, roughly 1500 to 500 BCE, during which the Vedas were composed. They are the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, and for most of that time they were transmitted orally, by memorised recitation, rather than written down.

The Rigveda, the oldest of the four, is a collection of over a thousand hymns to gods including Indra, Agni and Varuna, composed in an archaic Sanskrit in the Punjab by people who kept cattle, drove chariots and were organised in tribes. The Yajurveda, Samaveda and Atharvaveda followed, along with the Brahmanas, which set out the sacrificial ritual in detail, and eventually the Upanishads, philosophical dialogues about the self and ultimate reality that mark the end of the period.

Over these centuries settlement moved east from the Punjab to the Ganges plain, iron came into use, agriculture intensified, and small chiefdoms consolidated into the kingdoms and republics of the sixth century BCE. The fourfold varna order (priests, warriors, producers, servants) appears in the late Rigveda and hardens afterwards. The religion of sacrifice described in these texts is the root from which [classical Hinduism](event:hinduism-solidifies) grew, and the questions raised in the Upanishads run directly into the teaching of the [Buddha](event:buddha) and of Mahavira.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedic_period).

name: Battle of Kadesh
summary: Egyptians under Ramesses II fought the Hittites to a draw; the peace that followed is the earliest surviving international treaty.
body:
The Battle of Kadesh was fought around 1274 BCE on the Orontes river in western Syria, between the Egyptian army of Ramesses II and the [Hittites](event:hittite-empire) under Muwatalli II. It is probably the largest chariot battle ever fought, and it is the earliest battle anywhere whose tactics and formations can be reconstructed in detail.

Ramesses advanced north in four divisions to retake the city of Kadesh. Two captured Bedouin, planted by the Hittites, told him that Muwatalli's army was still far to the north; in fact it was concealed behind the city. The Hittite chariotry struck the second Egyptian division on the march and broke it, and Ramesses' own camp was overrun. He rallied with his household troops and the arrival of a further Egyptian force, and drove the Hittite chariots back against the river.

Both kings claimed victory. Neither took the field again that year, Kadesh stayed in Hittite hands, and Egyptian control in Syria was not restored. Sixteen years later the two powers concluded a formal peace, the earliest international treaty whose text survives; it exists in an Egyptian version carved at Karnak and a Hittite version on clay from Hattusa, and a copy hangs at the United Nations headquarters. Ramesses had his own account of the battle inscribed on temple walls across Egypt.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kadesh).

name: Iron Age begins
summary: Ironworking spread from Anatolia across Eurasia and Africa, putting hard metal within reach of ordinary farmers and soldiers.
body:
The Iron Age is the period in which iron and steel replaced bronze as the principal metal for tools and weapons. It began in the eastern Mediterranean and the Near East around 1200 BCE, after the [Late Bronze Age collapse](event:bronze-age-collapse), and reached different regions at very different dates: India by about 1200 BCE, China around 600 BCE, northern Europe later still.

Iron is harder to work than bronze. Its ore melts far above the temperatures ancient furnaces could reach, so it was produced as a spongy bloom that had to be hammered repeatedly to drive out slag, and plain wrought iron is softer than good bronze. What made it worth the effort was carburising and quenching, which turn the surface into steel, and above all supply: iron ore is common almost everywhere, while tin had to be fetched from a handful of distant sources.

That changed who could arm and equip themselves. Iron put hard edges within reach of ordinary farmers and of armies far larger than the chariot elites of the [Bronze Age](event:bronze-age), and iron axes and ploughshares opened heavy soils and woodland to cultivation. In Africa, ironworking spread [south of the Sahara](event:african-iron-working) without a preceding bronze age. The period ends by convention with the arrival of written history in each region.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Age).

name: Late Bronze Age collapse
summary: Within about fifty years the Hittite empire, Mycenaean Greece and the great trading cities of the Levant were all destroyed or abandoned.
body:
Between about 1200 and 1150 BCE the palace civilisations of the eastern Mediterranean and the Near East collapsed within roughly two generations. The [Hittite Empire](event:hittite-empire) ended, the [Mycenaean](event:mycenaean-greece) palaces burned, and the trading cities of the Levant, Cyprus and the Syrian coast were destroyed or abandoned. Egypt survived, but withdrew from the Levant and never recovered its former reach.

Almost every major city between Pylos and Gaza shows a destruction layer. Hattusa was burned and emptied; Ugarit fell, leaving letters in the kiln recording ships offshore and no troops to meet them; Egyptian records of Ramesses III describe fighting off a coalition of seaborne 'Sea Peoples' in his eighth year. Long-distance trade in copper, tin and luxuries stopped, and the administrative systems that depended on it stopped with it.

No single cause is accepted. Prolonged drought is now well attested in pollen and isotope records; earthquake swarms, migration and raiding, the spread of iron weapons and massed infantry, and internal revolt have all been argued; so has systems collapse, in which tightly interlocked and highly specialised economies fail together once one part gives way. Greece lost literacy altogether for some four centuries. Out of the aftermath came the Iron Age kingdoms of the Levant, the Neo-Assyrian revival and, eventually, the Greek city-states.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Bronze_Age_collapse).

steps.name: The Mycenaean palaces burn
steps.page: Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos and Thebes were destroyed or abandoned over a few decades. The Linear B tablets survive only because the fires that ended the archives baked them; the Pylos tablets record coastguards being posted shortly before the end. Greece lost writing, monumental building and long-distance trade together, and did not recover any of them for four centuries.

steps.name: Hattusa burned and abandoned
steps.page: The Hittite capital was emptied of its valuables and its archives before it burned, which suggests an orderly evacuation rather than a storm. Hittite central authority ended with it, and Anatolia fragmented. Successor Syro-Hittite states around Carchemish carried the name and the script on for several centuries.

steps.name: Ugarit destroyed
steps.page: Ugarit, a wealthy Syrian port and a hub of the Bronze Age trade in copper and grain, was burned and never reoccupied. Its last letters, found unfired in the kiln, report enemy ships burning towns along the coast while the city's own fleet and army were away in Lycia and Hatti.

steps.name: Ramesses III fights the Sea Peoples
steps.page: Reliefs and inscriptions at Medinet Habu describe Egypt defeating a coalition of seaborne and land-borne peoples (the Peleset, Tjeker, Shekelesh, Denyen and Weshesh) in Ramesses III's eighth year, about 1177 BCE. Who they were and where they came from is unresolved; they are as likely a symptom of the collapse as its cause. Egypt held, but lost its Levantine possessions.

steps.name: The aftermath
steps.page: By the middle of the twelfth century BCE the interconnected world of the Late Bronze Age was gone: no palace archives, no international correspondence between great kings, no bulk trade in tin. Egypt turned inward under the late Ramessides, Assyria contracted, and Greece entered a dark age. The Iron Age societies that emerged were smaller and poorer, and because [iron ore](event:iron-age) is common almost everywhere they depended less on long-distance supply.

name: Chinese oracle bone divination
summary: Ox scapulae and turtle shells inscribed for divination by the Shang carry the earliest known Chinese writing.
body:
Part of [Shang dynasty](event:shang-dynasty). Oracle bones are the ox shoulder blades and turtle plastrons that [Shang](event:shang-dynasty) diviners used to put questions to the royal ancestors, from about 1250 BCE. The inscriptions cut into them are the earliest known [Chinese writing](event:writing) and the earliest written records from East Asia.

The procedure was standardised. The bone was cleaned, thinned and drilled with hollows on the reverse; a hot point was applied to a hollow until the bone cracked with an audible pop; the pattern of the crack was read as the ancestors' answer. The charge (usually a paired statement and its negation, such as 'it will rain' and 'it will not rain') was then inscribed beside the crack, sometimes with the diviner's name, the date, the king's reading and, occasionally, what actually happened.

More than 150,000 pieces have been recovered, most from the Shang capital at Anyang. They ask about harvests, rain, hunting, illness, childbirth, military campaigns, sacrifices and the meaning of dreams, and they preserve a royal genealogy that closely matches the one in Sima Qian's history written a thousand years later. The script is already fully developed, with several thousand signs, roughly a third of them securely read; it is directly ancestral to modern Chinese characters. The bones were identified in 1899, having previously been ground up and sold as 'dragon bones' for medicine.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oracle_bone_script).

name: Trojan War
summary: The legendary siege of Troy, dated by later Greeks to the twelfth century BCE and immortalised in the *Iliad*.
body:
Part of [Late Bronze Age collapse](event:bronze-age-collapse). The Trojan War is the legendary conflict in which a coalition of Greek kingdoms besieged the city of Troy in north-western Anatolia. Later Greeks treated it as history and dated it to the twelfth century BCE (Eratosthenes put its end at 1184 BCE), and it was the central story of their literature and art.

In the legend, Paris of Troy carries off Helen, wife of Menelaus of Sparta; Agamemnon of Mycenae leads a thousand ships to recover her; the siege lasts ten years and ends with the wooden horse and the sack of the city. Homer's *Iliad* narrates a few weeks of the tenth year and the quarrel of Achilles and Agamemnon; the *Odyssey* follows one Greek home. The lost poems of the Epic Cycle covered the rest, and Greek tragedy and Roman epic worked the material over for centuries.

Whether any historical event lies behind it is unsettled. Heinrich Schliemann's excavations from 1870 at Hisarlik, now generally accepted as the site of Troy, exposed a mound of nine superimposed cities; the layers designated Troy VI and VIIa are of the right date and show destruction, though by what is unclear. Hittite documents mention a place called Wilusa and a power called Ahhiyawa, which many identify with Ilios and the [Achaeans](event:mycenaean-greece).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trojan_War).

name: Kingdom of Kush rises in Nubia
summary: A Nubian kingdom on the upper Nile rivalled Egypt, ruled it as the 25th Dynasty, and built hundreds of steep pyramids of its own.
body:
Kush was a Nubian kingdom on the upper Nile, in what is now northern Sudan, which rose as Egyptian power in the region receded after about 1070 BCE and lasted until roughly 350 CE. For most of a century it ruled Egypt itself as the Twenty-fifth Dynasty.

The kingdom formed around Napata, below the fourth cataract, where its kings adopted Egyptian titles, script and the cult of Amun at Jebel Barkal. From about 744 BCE Kashta and then Piye moved north and took Egypt, and Kushite pharaohs ruled from the Delta to the confluence of the Niles, restoring temples and reviving Old Kingdom artistic styles. Assyrian invasions drove them out in the 660s BCE.

The court later moved south to Meroë, between the fifth and sixth cataracts, beyond the reach of Egyptian armies and in better farming and grazing country. Meroë smelted iron on a large scale and traded gold, ivory, ebony, incense and animals north to Egypt and the Mediterranean and east to the Red Sea. Kushite rulers were buried under hundreds of steep, small pyramids at el-Kurru, Nuri and Meroë, more pyramids than Egypt has. In the Meroitic phase the kingdom wrote its own language in its own [script](event:meroitic-script), and several ruling queens held the title *kandake*.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Kush).

steps.name: The kingdom forms at Napata
steps.page: With Egypt's New Kingdom empire gone from Nubia, a local dynasty consolidated power around Napata, below the fourth cataract. Its rulers took Egyptian royal titles and buried their dead under pyramids at el-Kurru, and they made the temple of Amun at Jebel Barkal the religious centre of the kingdom.

steps.name: Kush takes Egypt: the 25th Dynasty
steps.page: Kashta moved north into Upper Egypt and Piye completed the conquest around 727 BCE, recording it on a granite stele at Jebel Barkal. Kushite pharaohs (Piye, Shabaka, Shebitku, Taharqa and Tanutamun) ruled from the Delta to the confluence of the Blue and White Niles, restored neglected temples, and revived Old Kingdom art and burial practice.

steps.name: Assyria drives Kush out of Egypt
steps.page: Esarhaddon invaded Egypt in 671 BCE and Ashurbanipal sacked Thebes in 663, ending Kushite rule in the north. The dynasty withdrew to Nubia. Egyptian kingship passed to the Saite Twenty-sixth Dynasty, backed by [Assyria](event:neo-assyrian).

steps.name: The capital moves to Meroë
steps.page: The royal court and, later, the royal cemetery shifted south to Meroë, above the fifth cataract, further from Egyptian armies, with more rainfall, better grazing and abundant iron ore and timber for smelting. Meroë became a large industrial and trading city, its slag heaps still visible.

steps.name: Kush and Rome
steps.page: Kushite forces raided Roman Egypt and carried off statues of Augustus from Aswan; a bronze head of the emperor was found buried beneath a temple threshold at Meroë, where it had been placed to be walked on. A Roman counter-expedition sacked Napata, and the two powers then settled a frontier and a peace that held for generations.

steps.name: Decline and the end of Meroë
steps.page: Trade shifted to the Red Sea and to the rising power of Aksum, the desert advanced, and the pyramid burials became poorer. An Aksumite inscription of the fourth century CE records a campaign against Meroë. The kingdom disappears from the record around 350 CE, and Nubia passed to the successor kingdoms of Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia.

name: Phoenician alphabet
summary: A script of about 22 consonant signs, simple enough for merchants to learn, spread around the Mediterranean.
body:
The Phoenician alphabet was a script of 22 consonant signs used from about the eleventh century BCE by the Phoenician city-states of the Levantine coast: Byblos, Tyre, Sidon. Nearly every alphabet in use today descends from it.

It was an abjad: each sign stood for a consonant, and vowels were left to the reader. Derived from earlier Proto-Sinaitic and Canaanite letters that were themselves adapted from Egyptian hieroglyphs, it reduced writing to a set small enough to be learned in days rather than the hundreds of signs a scribe of cuneiform or hieroglyphic had to master. Writing stopped being the property of a professional caste, and merchants could keep their own accounts.

Phoenician traders and colonists carried it around the Mediterranean. The [Greeks](event:greek-alphabet) adopted it around 800 BCE and reassigned several signs they did not need to vowels, producing the first true alphabet; from Greek came Etruscan and then Latin, and later Cyrillic. Aramaic, which took over as the administrative language of the Near East, produced the Hebrew, Syriac and Arabic scripts and, through Brahmi, most of the scripts of South and South-East Asia. The letter names and their order survive: *aleph, bet, gimel* is still A, B, C and alpha, beta, gamma.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenician_alphabet).

name: Zhou Dynasty
summary: China's longest dynasty, which introduced the 'Mandate of Heaven' and presided over the classical age of Chinese philosophy.
body:
The Zhou was the longest-lasting dynasty in Chinese history, ruling from about 1046 to 256 BCE. It overthrew the [Shang](event:shang-dynasty), justified the conquest with the doctrine of the Mandate of Heaven, and presided, latterly in name only, over the period in which classical Chinese thought took shape.

The Mandate of Heaven held that heaven granted the right to rule to a virtuous king and withdrew it from a cruel or negligent one, at which point rebellion became legitimate. It supplied Chinese politics with a theory of dynastic change that lasted into the twentieth century. The early Zhou governed through kinsmen and allies enfeoffed with territories, an arrangement often compared to European feudalism, held together by ritual and by the king's prestige.

In 771 BCE the capital was sacked and the court fled east to Luoyang. Real power passed to the regional states, and the Eastern Zhou is conventionally divided into the Spring and Autumn period and the Warring States period, each more violent than the last. That disorder was also the setting for the 'hundred schools of thought': [Confucius](event:confucius), Laozi, Mozi, Mencius, Zhuangzi and the Legalists all wrote in it, and their arguments about government, ritual and human nature became the foundation of Chinese philosophy. The Zhou line was extinguished in 256 BCE, and [Qin](event:qin-unification) completed the conquest of the rest.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhou_dynasty).

steps.name: The Zhou overthrow the Shang at Muye
steps.page: King Wu of Zhou defeated the last Shang king at Muye, traditionally in 1046 BCE. The Zhou justified the conquest by announcing that heaven had withdrawn its mandate from a debauched ruler and given it to them. The doctrine was invoked at every later change of dynasty.

steps.name: The Western Zhou settlement
steps.page: After King Wu's early death, the Duke of Zhou put down a revolt and organised the new state: relatives and allies were granted territories on condition of military service and tribute, a second capital was founded at Luoyang, and an elaborate ritual order fixed rank and obligation. Bronze vessels cast with long inscriptions record the grants.

steps.name: The court flees east to Luoyang
steps.page: In 771 BCE the Zhou capital in the Wei valley was sacked by Quanrong tribesmen with the help of disaffected nobles, and King You was killed. His successor moved the court east to Luoyang. The Eastern Zhou kings kept their ritual primacy but lost the land and armies that had backed it.

steps.name: The Spring and Autumn period
steps.page: Named after the chronicle of the state of Lu, this is the age of the hegemons: powerful rulers such as Duke Huan of Qi who convened the other states and acted in the Zhou king's name. Over 250 years the number of polities fell from some hundreds to a dozen or so through conquest and absorption.

steps.name: The Warring States period
steps.page: Seven large states fought for supremacy with mass conscript infantry, crossbows, iron weapons and siege warfare, and reorganised themselves internally to sustain it: bureaucracies, land taxes, registered populations. It was also the period in which the Confucian, Daoist, Mohist and Legalist schools argued out their positions.

steps.name: The last Zhou king
steps.page: Qin annexed the Zhou royal domain and deposed King Nan in 256 BCE, ending the dynasty as a political fact centuries after it had ceased to be one in practice. Qin then finished the conquest of the remaining states, completing the [unification](event:qin-unification) in 221 BCE.

name: Solomon's Temple in Jerusalem
summary: The First Temple was built in Jerusalem, becoming the centre of Israelite worship until its destruction in 587 BCE.
body:
Solomon's Temple, or the First Temple, was the temple in Jerusalem described in the Hebrew Bible as built by King Solomon in the tenth century BCE to house the Ark of the Covenant. It served as the central sanctuary of Israelite worship until it was destroyed by the Babylonians in 587 BCE.

The biblical account in the Books of Kings and Chronicles is detailed: a rectangular building on the eastern hill of the city, entered through a porch flanked by two bronze pillars, with an outer hall and an inner Holy of Holies housing the Ark under the wings of two great cherubim, and cedar supplied by Hiram of Tyre. No archaeological trace of the building has been found, and none is likely to be: the Temple Mount cannot be excavated. Historians differ on how much of the account reflects a tenth-century structure and how much a later one.

Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon took Jerusalem, burned the temple and deported much of the population; the [Hebrew scriptures](event:hebrew-bible-canon) were largely compiled and edited in and after that exile. A Second Temple was built on the site from 516 BCE, greatly enlarged by Herod, and destroyed by Rome in 70 CE. The Western Wall is a surviving retaining wall of Herod's platform, and the site remains central to Judaism and, as the Haram al-Sharif, to Islam.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solomon%27s_Temple).

name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
summary: Assyria built the largest empire the world had yet seen, ruling from Nineveh with siege engines, mass deportation and a road system.
body:
The Neo-Assyrian Empire, from about 911 to 609 BCE, was the largest state the world had yet seen. At its height under Ashurbanipal it ran from Egypt and Cyprus to the Persian Gulf and the Zagros, ruled from Nineveh on the Tigris.

Assyrian power rested on a professional standing army, the first in history to be equipped mainly with iron, and on siege engineering (battering rams, ramps, sapping and towers) that could take walled cities other armies could only blockade. It rested equally on administration: provinces under appointed governors rather than tributary kings, a royal road with relay stations for messengers, standardised taxation, and a corps of scribes and informers reporting to the palace. Conquered populations were deported wholesale and resettled far from home, a policy that broke local resistance and moved skills where the state wanted them; the deportation of Israel after the fall of Samaria in 722 BCE is the best-known case.

Assyrian kings recorded their campaigns in palace reliefs and annals, including detailed depictions of the violence involved. Ashurbanipal also assembled at Nineveh the largest library of the ancient Near East, whose tablets, including the fullest text of the Epic of Gilgamesh, survived because the palace burned. Overextended and worn down by civil war, the empire fell within a generation to a coalition of Babylonians and Medes.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Assyrian_Empire).

steps.name: Assyria recovers under Adad-nirari II
steps.page: After two centuries of contraction, Adad-nirari II began the annual campaigning that would recover the Assyrian heartland and the trade routes of upper Mesopotamia. His reign is the conventional start of the Neo-Assyrian period.

steps.name: Ashurnasirpal II builds Kalhu
steps.page: Ashurnasirpal II pushed Assyrian arms to the Mediterranean and moved the capital to Kalhu (Nimrud), where he built a palace lined with carved stone reliefs of hunts, battles and deportations. An inscription records a ten-day banquet for nearly 70,000 guests at its dedication.

steps.name: Tiglath-Pileser III remakes the empire
steps.page: Tiglath-Pileser III converted a system of tribute-paying vassals into directly governed provinces, broke up the great commands that had threatened the throne, reorganised the army around professional and conscript units, and made mass deportation routine policy. Most of what the empire became dates from his reign.

steps.name: The fall of Samaria
steps.page: The northern kingdom of Israel was annexed after a three-year siege of its capital and its population deported into upper Mesopotamia and Media. Judah survived as a tributary. The episode is recorded both in Assyrian annals and in the Hebrew Bible, where the deportees become the 'lost tribes'.

steps.name: Sennacherib and Nineveh
steps.page: Sennacherib made Nineveh the capital, rebuilding it with an aqueduct, canals and a 'palace without rival' whose reliefs show the siege of Lachish in detail. His campaign against Judah in 701 BCE left Jerusalem paying a heavy indemnity. He destroyed Babylon in 689 BCE, an act his own successors treated as sacrilege.

steps.name: The conquest of Egypt
steps.page: Esarhaddon took Memphis in 671 BCE and Ashurbanipal sacked Thebes in 663, ending the [Kushite](event:nubian-kush) Twenty-fifth Dynasty and bringing the empire to its greatest extent. Egypt proved impossible to hold and was lost within a decade.

steps.name: Nineveh falls
steps.page: A coalition of Babylonians under Nabopolassar and Medes under Cyaxares took Ashur in 614 BCE and Nineveh in 612, after the empire had exhausted itself in a civil war between Ashurbanipal's heirs. The city was sacked and never recovered.

steps.name: The last stand at Harran
steps.page: A remnant Assyrian court held out at Harran with Egyptian support and was finally destroyed in 609 BCE. Assyria disappeared as a state; its territory passed to the Neo-Babylonian empire, and from there, within a lifetime, to [Persia](event:achaemenid-empire).

name: Founding of Carthage
summary: Phoenician settlers from Tyre founded the city that became the dominant power of the western Mediterranean.
body:
Carthage was founded by Phoenician settlers from Tyre on the coast of what is now Tunisia. Tradition, reported by Greek and Roman writers, dates the founding to 814 BCE and credits it to the exiled Tyrian princess Elissa, called Dido by the Romans; the earliest archaeological material from the site is of the eighth century BCE.

Its position on a promontory commanding the narrows between Sicily and Africa made it the natural centre of the western Mediterranean trade in metals, textiles, salt fish and slaves. As Tyre came under Assyrian and then Babylonian pressure, Carthage took over the western Phoenician network for itself: colonies and trading posts in North Africa, Sardinia, western Sicily and southern Spain, and voyages beyond the Strait of Gibraltar. It was governed as a republic by two annually elected magistrates, a senate and an assembly, an arrangement Aristotle discussed with approval.

Its wealth came from commerce and from the farmland of its African hinterland, and its wars were fought largely by mercenaries and allied contingents rather than citizen levies. Long rivalry with the Greeks over Sicily gave way to conflict with Rome in the [Punic Wars](event:punic-wars), which ended in 146 BCE with the city destroyed and its territory annexed. A Roman colony was refounded on the site a century later and became one of the largest cities of the empire.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage).

name: Greek alphabet emerges
summary: Greeks adapted the Phoenician script, added signs for vowels, and produced the ancestor of the Western alphabets.
body:
Part of [Phoenician alphabet](event:phoenician-alphabet). The Greek alphabet has been in use since the late ninth or early eighth century BCE, adapted from the [Phoenician](event:phoenician-alphabet) script. It is the earliest known writing system to record vowels as systematically as consonants, and it is the ancestor of the Latin and Cyrillic alphabets.

Phoenician was an abjad: 22 consonant signs, with the vowels supplied by the reader. Greek has vowels that carry meaning and could not be written that way. Signs for Semitic sounds Greek did not use (aleph, he, yod, ayin and waw) were reassigned to a, e, i, o and u, and later additions gave the standard 24 letters. The result records speech closely enough that a reader who knows the letters can sound out a word never seen before.

The earliest samples date from at least 775 BCE; the oldest substantial inscriptions, on the Dipylon jug and on 'Nestor's Cup', are from about 740–730 BCE, and both are scratched on ordinary pots rather than cut for a king. Cities used differing local varieties until Athens adopted the Ionic form officially in 403 BCE. From the western variants came the Etruscan and then the Latin alphabet; from the eastern came Coptic, Gothic and Cyrillic.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_alphabet).

name: First Olympic Games
summary: The traditional date of the first games at Olympia, which the Greeks used as the origin of their shared chronology.
body:
By tradition the first Olympic Games were held in 776 BCE at the sanctuary of Olympia, in the western Peloponnese, in honour of Zeus. They were held every four years, and Greek writers later counted dates by Olympiads, which gave the Greek world its first shared chronology.

The festival combined athletics with sacrifice and procession, and the sanctuary itself, with its great temple of Zeus and the chryselephantine statue by Phidias inside it, was as important to the occasion as the competition. For the first thirteen Olympiads the only event was the stadion, a sprint of about 192 metres; longer races, wrestling, boxing, the pankration, the pentathlon and chariot and horse racing were added over the following centuries. Victors were crowned with a wreath of wild olive, and were rewarded at home with money, statues and privileges.

A truce, the ekecheiria, was proclaimed before each festival so that competitors and spectators could travel safely through territories at war. Three other panhellenic festivals (the Pythian, Nemean and Isthmian games) were founded on the same model in the sixth century BCE. The games continued under Roman rule and were suppressed in the late fourth century CE, as the empire became Christian; the modern Olympics were founded in 1896 in conscious imitation.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Olympic_Games).

name: Founding of Rome
summary: Traditional date of Rome's founding, from which the Romans afterwards numbered their years.
body:
Roman tradition dated the founding of the city to 753 BCE, a date calculated in the first century BCE by the scholar Varro and used thereafter to number years *ab urbe condita*, from the founding of the city. The legend attached to it makes Romulus the founder and first king.

In the story, the twins Romulus and Remus, sons of Mars and descendants of the Trojan Aeneas, were exposed as infants, suckled by a she-wolf and raised by a herdsman. Quarrelling over where to build, Romulus killed his brother and gave the city his name. Six kings were said to have followed him, the last three of them Etruscan, until the monarchy was overthrown and the [Republic](event:roman-republic-founded) established in 509 BCE.

Archaeology tells a slower story. There were huts on the Palatine hill by the tenth century BCE and burials in the Forum valley from about the same time. Separate settlements on the hills appear to have merged over the eighth and seventh centuries, with the draining of the marshy Forum and the building of a defensive wall marking the point at which a town rather than a group of villages existed. The legend was shaped later, under [Etruscan](event:etruscan-influence) and Greek influence, and given its standard form by [Virgil](event:virgil-aeneid) and Livy under Augustus.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_of_Rome).

name: Etruscan civilisation influences Rome
summary: The Etruscans of central Italy shaped early Roman religion, government, architecture and culture.
body:
The Etruscans occupied Etruria (modern Tuscany, western Umbria and northern Lazio) and were the dominant power in central Italy from about the eighth to the fourth century BCE. Rome grew up on their southern edge, and much of early Roman religion, engineering and public display came from them.

They lived in a loose league of independent cities: Veii, Caere, Tarquinia, Vulci, Clusium and others, rich on Tuscan copper and iron and on trade with Greeks and Phoenicians. Their language, written in an alphabet borrowed from the Greeks, was not Indo-European and is still only partly understood, since almost everything that survives is short funerary inscriptions. Their painted chamber tombs are the best evidence of how they lived.

Roman tradition made three of the seven kings Etruscan, among them Tarquinius Superbus, whose expulsion in 509 BCE begins the [Republic](event:roman-republic-founded). From Etruria Rome took divination by the flight of birds and by the livers of sacrificed animals, the podium temple with its deep porch, the Cloaca Maxima that drained the Forum, the fasces carried before magistrates, the triumph and the toga. The alphabet reached Latin through Etruscan hands. Rome absorbed the cities one by one after the fall of Veii in 396 BCE, and Etruscan died out in the early empire.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etruscan_civilization).

name: Early Greek philosophers
summary: Thales, Pythagoras, Heraclitus and others sought natural explanations for the world rather than mythological ones.
body:
The Presocratics were the first Greek thinkers to look for explanations of the world in the world itself rather than in the acts of the gods. They worked from about 600 BCE in the Ionian cities of the Anatolian coast and in the Greek colonies of southern Italy and Sicily, not in Athens, and their writings survive only as fragments quoted by later authors.

Thales of Miletus, credited by Herodotus with predicting the solar eclipse of 585 BCE, held that everything is ultimately water. His successors argued for other principles: Anaximander for an indefinite *apeiron*, Anaximenes for air. Heraclitus of Ephesus made change itself the constant and set reason, *logos*, behind it; Parmenides of Elea argued the opposite, that change is an illusion and being is one, and forced everyone after him to answer the argument. Pythagoras, who moved from Samos to Croton, founded a religious brotherhood around the claim that number and ratio underlie music and the cosmos.

Later Presocratics answered Parmenides with pluralism: Empedocles' four roots moved by love and strife, Anaxagoras' universal mind, and the atoms and void of Leucippus and Democritus, the ancestor of every later atomic theory. Their common assumption, that the world has causes which argument can reach, is why they are regarded as the first Western philosophers.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presocratic_philosophy).

name: Zoroastrianism in Persia
summary: An ancient Persian faith, dualist in outlook, whose ideas of a final judgment are often argued to have influenced Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
body:
Zoroastrianism is the religion founded on the teaching of the Iranian priest Zarathushtra, known in Greek as Zoroaster. It centres on one creator god, Ahura Mazda, and on a moral order in which truth stands against the lie and every person's choice matters to the outcome.

Zoroaster's own date is not settled: the archaic language of the Gathas, the hymns attributed to him, points to somewhere between about 1500 and 1000 BCE, while Greek and later Iranian tradition placed him much later, in the seventh or sixth century. His hymns form the oldest layer of the Avesta, the scripture, which was transmitted orally for centuries before being written down. Worship centres on a tended fire as the symbol of purity, and the ethical formula is good thoughts, good words, good deeds.

The kings of the [Achaemenid Empire](event:achaemenid-empire) invoked Ahura Mazda in their inscriptions, and under the Sasanians, from the third century CE, Zoroastrianism was the state religion of Persia with an organised priesthood. It declined after the Arab conquest of the seventh century; communities survive in Iran and, as the Parsis, in India. Its doctrines of a final judgment, an afterlife of reward and punishment, a saviour and a bodily resurrection are widely argued to have influenced Second Temple Judaism and, through it, Christianity and Islam.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoroastrianism).

name: Life of the Buddha
summary: Siddhartha Gautama taught in the Ganges plain, founding one of the world's great religious and philosophical traditions.
body:
Siddhartha Gautama, later called the Buddha ('the awakened one'), was a teacher who lived in the eastern Ganges plain and founded the community and the body of teaching that became Buddhism. Tradition places his life in 563–483 BCE; much modern scholarship dates his death a century later, between about 480 and 400 BCE.

He was born into the Shakya clan at Lumbini, in what is now Nepal, the son of a local ruler. The traditional life has him leaving his family and household at twenty-nine, studying under teachers of meditation and then practising severe asceticism for six years, and abandoning both extremes for what he called the middle way. He reached awakening in meditation under a tree at Bodh Gaya, and gave his first discourse in the deer park at Sarnath near Varanasi.

His teaching is summarised in the Four Noble Truths: that existence involves suffering, that suffering arises from craving, that it can cease, and that a path leads to its cessation, the Noble Eightfold Path of right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration. He taught that nothing has a permanent self and that all things arise in dependence on conditions. He accepted no caste distinction among his followers.

He taught for some forty-five years across Magadha and Kosala, and organised a monastic community, the sangha, which outlived him. He died at Kushinagar, aged about eighty. His words were preserved by recitation and not written down for several centuries, first in the Pali Canon. Under [Ashoka](event:maurya-empire) the religion spread beyond India, and it later travelled the [Silk Road](event:spread-buddhism) into Central Asia and China.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gautama_Buddha).

name: Confucius
summary: Kong Qiu taught an ethic of duty, ritual propriety and learning that shaped Chinese government and society for two millennia.
body:
Part of [Zhou Dynasty](event:zhou-dynasty). Confucius (Kong Qiu, honorifically Kongzi, 'Master Kong') was a Chinese teacher and official who lived from 551 to 479 BCE, in the Spring and Autumn period of the [Zhou](event:zhou-dynasty), when the royal house had lost authority and the states fought among themselves. He taught that order is restored by cultivating character, not by force, and his ideas became the working philosophy of the Chinese state.

He was born in the small state of Lu, in modern Shandong, held minor office there, and spent much of his later life travelling from court to court in search of a ruler who would apply his ideas. None did. He is said to have taught some three thousand students, and to have taken pupils regardless of their birth.

His central terms are *ren*, humaneness or fellow feeling; *li*, the ritual propriety that governs how people treat one another; *xiao*, devotion to parents; and the *junzi*, the exemplary person, a title he redefined from noble birth to moral quality. Government, he held, works by the example the ruler sets: correct names, correct conduct, and the people follow. He described himself as a transmitter rather than an innovator, appealing to the practice of the early Zhou.

The *Analects*, a collection of his sayings and conversations, was compiled by later followers. Mencius and Xunzi developed the tradition in opposite directions; the Qin suppressed it; the [Han](event:han-dynasty) made it official, and from the seventh century CE the Confucian classics were the syllabus of the imperial examinations that selected officials until 1905.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confucius).

name: Achaemenid Persian Empire
summary: Cyrus the Great and his successors ruled from the Aegean to the Indus, the largest empire the world had seen.
body:
The Achaemenid Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great about 550 BCE, was the first Persian empire and the largest state the world had yet seen. At its height it ran from the Aegean and Egypt to the Indus, and it was governed as a single administrative system rather than as a collection of tributaries.

Cyrus overthrew his Median overlord, took Lydia and the Greek cities of Ionia in 547 BCE, and entered Babylon in 539. The Cyrus Cylinder records his restoration of local cults; the Hebrew Bible remembers him for allowing the Judean exiles to return and rebuild the temple. His son Cambyses II added Egypt in 525. Darius I, who seized the throne in 522 and justified it in the trilingual Behistun inscription, reorganised the empire into some twenty satrapies, each under a governor watched by royal inspectors, with fixed tribute in silver, a standard gold coin (the daric), an imperial post and the Royal Road running some 2,700 km from Sardis to Susa. Aramaic served as the language of administration. Persepolis was begun as a ceremonial capital, alongside Susa, Ecbatana and Babylon.

The empire held perhaps forty million people, a large share of the world's population at the time, and generally let subject peoples keep their languages, laws and religions. Its western expansion failed against the Greek city-states in the [Greco-Persian Wars](event:greco-persian-wars). It fell in four years to [Alexander](event:alexander-conquests): Gaugamela in 331 BCE, Persepolis burned the following year, and Darius III killed by his own satrap in 330.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire).

name: Roman Republic formally established
summary: Rome replaced its kings with elected magistrates and citizen assemblies, a constitution that lasted nearly five centuries.
body:
The Roman Republic was the form of government at Rome between the end of the monarchy and the rule of Augustus, traditionally 509 to 27 BCE. Power was held by annually elected magistrates and by the Senate, and no one man was supposed to hold it for long.

Tradition dates the founding to the expulsion of the last king, Tarquinius Superbus, by Lucius Junius Brutus; historians see a slower drift away from monarchy over the sixth and fifth centuries. The constitution developed piecemeal rather than by design. Two consuls, elected for a single year, each able to veto the other, held military and civil authority; below them, praetors judged, censors registered citizens and let contracts, quaestors handled money. The Senate, a standing body of former magistrates, controlled finance and foreign policy by custom rather than by law, and assemblies of citizens elected magistrates and passed statutes.

The Conflict of the Orders, from the fifth century, forced the patrician families to share power with the plebeians: tribunes of the plebs with the power to block any act of a magistrate, the publication of the Twelve Tables about 450 BCE, and eventually plebeian access to every office. The result was a system of overlapping checks that Polybius admired as a mixture of monarchy, aristocracy and democracy.

It governed Rome through the [Punic Wars](event:punic-wars) and the conquest of the Mediterranean, and broke down in the first century BCE. Later republics (the Italian city-states, the Dutch, the American) studied its vocabulary and its offices closely.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic).

name: Athenian democracy
summary: The reforms of Cleisthenes gave political power to the assembly of citizens, inventing direct democracy.
body:
