Athenian democracy was the system under which the citizens of Athens governed themselves directly, from the reforms of Cleisthenes in 508/507 BCE until the city lost its independence in 322 BCE. It is the first political system known to have been called a democracy, and the first for which the workings are documented in detail.

Cleisthenes broke the hold of the aristocratic clans by reorganising the citizen body into ten new tribes, each drawn from villages in three separate parts of Attica so that no tribe was a regional faction. A Council of 500, fifty from each tribe and chosen by lot for a year, prepared business; the Assembly, open to every adult male citizen, met about forty times a year on the Pnyx to decide it. Ephialtes stripped the old aristocratic council of the Areopagus of its political powers in 462 BCE, and under Pericles the state paid jurors, and later assembly-goers, so that poorer citizens could attend.

Selection by lot rather than election was central: it treated any citizen as competent to judge, and only the generalships and a few technical offices were filled by vote. Ostracism allowed the Assembly to exile a citizen for ten years without charge.

The citizen body numbered perhaps 30,000 adult men out of a population of some 250,000. Women, resident foreigners and a large enslaved population had no vote. The system was overthrown twice during the [Peloponnesian War](event:peloponnesian-war) and restored both times; it ended after the Lamian War, when Macedon imposed a property qualification. The idea it began is treated in [democracy](item:democracy).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athenian_democracy).

name: Democracy
summary: Rule by the people: the principle that political authority derives from those subject to it, and the institutions built to make that workable.
body:
The word is Greek, and so is the first documented example. The reforms of Cleisthenes in 508 BCE reorganised [Athens](item:athenian-democracy) so that policy was decided by an assembly of citizens and offices were filled largely by lot. It was direct, not representative, and the citizen body excluded women, resident foreigners and a very large enslaved population, and perhaps a seventh of the adults present had a vote.

The Athenian institution did not survive antiquity, but its vocabulary did. Roman republicanism, the limits placed on a king by [Magna Carta](item:magna-carta), and the Dutch and English revolutions supplied the vocabulary of consent, representation and the rule of law; the [American](item:us-constitution) and [French](item:rights-of-man) revolutions turned it into written constitutions asserting rights against the state.

The franchise widened slowly and unevenly: property qualifications, then [women's suffrage](item:finland-suffrage) from 1906, then the [American civil rights](item:civil-rights-act) legislation of the 1960s and the [end of apartheid](item:apartheid-end) in 1994. The count of electoral democracies rose through the twentieth century and has fallen back since about 2010.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy).

name: Hinduism takes classical form
summary: The Vedas, Upanishads and Puranas set out the cosmology, deities and rituals of Hinduism over the course of a millennium.
body:
Between roughly 500 BCE and 500 CE the religious traditions of northern India took the shape now called classical Hinduism: the epics and Puranas, the philosophical schools, the law books, temple worship and the great deities Vishnu, Shiva and the Goddess.

The [Vedic period](event:vedic-period) had left a religion of sacrifice conducted by priests. The Upanishads turned the enquiry inward, to the self and its identity with ultimate reality, and the ascetic movements of the sixth century BCE (including [Buddhism](event:buddha) and Jainism) challenged the authority of the Vedas and of the priesthood outright.

The two Sanskrit epics, the *Mahabharata* and the *Ramayana*, were composed and expanded over these centuries; the *Bhagavad Gita*, a dialogue set within the *Mahabharata*, reconciled duty, knowledge and devotion to a personal god. The Puranas supplied cosmology and the mythology of the major deities. Six schools of philosophy (among them Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa and Vedanta) were systematised in terse aphorisms and their commentaries. The Dharmashastra literature, including the *Manusmriti*, set out law and the duties of the four varnas and the stages of life.

Worship shifted from the open-air fire altar to the image in a temple, and devotion (*bhakti*) to a chosen god became a path in its own right. The doctrines of dharma, karma and rebirth were common ground across all of it. 'Hinduism' itself is a much later name for the whole.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinduism).

name: Hebrew Bible canon formed
summary: Jewish scholars collected and standardised the Torah, Prophets and Writings, settling a canon that later communities preserved.
body:
The Hebrew Bible, or Tanakh, is the collection of Jewish scriptures in three parts: the Torah, the Prophets and the Writings. It was assembled and fixed over several centuries, roughly between the return from the Babylonian exile and the second century CE.

The Torah, the five books of Moses, was substantially complete by about 400 BCE, under Persian rule, when the exiles' descendants rebuilt Jerusalem and its temple. The Prophets, the historical books together with the prophetic collections, followed over the next two centuries. The Writings, a mixed group including Psalms, Proverbs, Job, Daniel and the five scrolls, closed last. The grandson of Ben Sira, writing about 130 BCE, already refers to 'the law, the prophets, and the other books', which shows the first two parts settled and the third still open.

A Greek translation, the Septuagint, was made in Alexandria from the third century BCE for Jews who no longer read Hebrew; it includes books the Hebrew canon left out. The Dead Sea Scrolls, copied between about 250 BCE and 70 CE, show that the wording of individual books still varied at that date; a single consonantal text became standard afterwards, and was fixed with vowel points by the Masoretes between the seventh and tenth centuries CE.

The same books, in a different order, form the Christian Old Testament, and the narratives and figures in them recur throughout the Quran.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_Bible).

name: Iron working spreads in sub-Saharan Africa
summary: Smelting furnaces appear across sub-Saharan Africa, from the Nok culture of Nigeria to the Great Lakes, changing farming and trade.
body:
Iron smelting was practised across sub-Saharan Africa in the first millennium BCE, from the Nok culture on the Jos plateau of Nigeria to the Great Lakes and, further north, the ironworking centres of [Kush](event:nubian-kush) at Meroë. Iron tools changed farming and, with it, where and how densely people could live.

Much of the region has no bronze age: it passed from stone tools to iron directly, which is one reason the question of origin is still argued. Some archaeologists hold that the technique was carried across the Sahara or up the Nile from the Mediterranean world; others argue for independent invention, citing very early dates from the Termit massif in Niger and from central Africa that remain contested on stratigraphic and radiocarbon grounds. Nok furnaces are securely dated to about 500 BCE, and Urewe ware in the Great Lakes region is associated with smelting from a similar date.

African smelters used tall natural-draught shaft furnaces, sometimes with bellows, built of clay and charged with charcoal and ore; a smelt was a communal undertaking, and smiths often held a ritual status set apart from other craftsmen. Iron hoes and axes made heavy soils and woodland ground workable, and iron weapons changed the balance between groups.

The spread of ironworking overlapped with the long Bantu migrations, which carried farming, cattle and Bantu languages from the Nigeria–Cameroon borderlands across central, eastern and southern Africa over some two thousand years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_metallurgy_in_Africa).

name: Greco-Persian Wars
summary: Half a century of conflict between the Persian Empire and the Greek city-states, which the Greeks ended without being conquered.
body:
The Greco-Persian Wars were fought between the [Achaemenid Empire](event:achaemenid-empire) and the Greek city-states from 499 to 449 BCE. Persia twice invaded mainland Greece and twice failed, and the Greek states then spent thirty years pushing Persian power back out of the Aegean.

The war began as a rebellion. The Greek cities of Ionia, on the Anatolian coast, had been Persian subjects for two generations; when they revolted, Athens and Eretria sent help, and an Athenian force took part in the burning of Sardis. Persia crushed the revolt and then turned on the mainland cities that had intervened. Two invasions followed, the first under generals sent by Darius I, the second led in person by his son Xerxes with an army and fleet assembled from across the empire.

The fighting is preserved in unusual detail because Herodotus wrote it down within living memory, and the campaign has been argued over by historians ever since, above all the Persian numbers, which Herodotus gives in millions and which modern estimates reduce by an order of magnitude.

Athens emerged with a fleet and with the leadership of an alliance that became an empire, funding the building of the [Parthenon](event:parthenon) and the public pay that sustained its [democracy](event:athenian-democracy). The wars became the founding story of a Greek identity defined against Persia, and, much later, of a European one.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco-Persian_Wars).

steps.name: The Ionian Revolt
steps.page: The Greek cities of Ionia rose against their Persian governors in 499 BCE. Athens and Eretria sent ships, and a raiding force burned Sardis, the seat of the western satrapy. Persia recovered the coast city by city and destroyed the Ionian fleet at Lade in 494; Miletus was sacked and its people deported.

steps.name: The first invasion of Greece
steps.page: Mardonius crossed to Thrace and Macedon in 492 BCE and lost much of his fleet off Mount Athos. Two years later Datis and Artaphernes sailed directly across the Aegean, sacked Eretria and deported its population, and landed in Attica to punish Athens for its part in the revolt.

steps.name: Xerxes' invasion
steps.page: Xerxes spent four years preparing, bridged the Hellespont with pontoons and cut a canal through the Athos peninsula. The army marched down through Thessaly in 480 BCE with the fleet alongside it. Thirty-one Greek states swore a common alliance at Corinth and gave command on land and sea to Sparta.

steps.name: Plataea and Mycale
steps.page: Xerxes went home after Salamis, leaving Mardonius with a picked army in Greece. In 479 BCE the largest Greek force yet assembled destroyed it at Plataea in Boeotia and killed Mardonius. The Greek fleet crossed to Mycale on the Ionian coast in the same season and burned the Persian ships drawn up there, and Ionia revolted again.

steps.name: The Delian League carries the war east
steps.page: Athens took over the leadership from Sparta in 478 BCE and organised the Aegean states into an alliance with its treasury on Delos. Over the next thirty years it cleared Persian garrisons from Thrace and the straits, destroyed a Persian army and fleet at the Eurymedon about 466, and lost a large expedition supporting a revolt in Egypt. Fighting stopped around 449, by tradition under a Peace of Callias whose existence ancient writers already doubted.

name: Battle of Marathon
summary: An outnumbered Athenian hoplite army defeated the Persian landing force on the plain of Marathon.
body:
Part of [Greco-Persian Wars](event:greco-persian-wars). The Battle of Marathon was fought in 490 BCE on the coastal plain of Marathon, some 40 km north-east of Athens, between an Athenian army and the Persian expedition sent by Darius I. The Athenians won, and the Persians withdrew by sea.

The expedition, under Datis and Artaphernes, was a punitive one: it had already destroyed Eretria for its part in the [Ionian Revolt](event:greco-persian-wars) and was to do the same to Athens. About 10,000 Athenians and 1,000 Plataeans marched out and blocked the exits from the plain. Sparta had promised help but would not march until a religious festival was over.

The Greeks held their position for several days and then attacked, according to Herodotus at a run over the last stretch to cross the archers' killing ground quickly. Their centre was thin and gave way; the strengthened wings held, turned inward and closed on the Persian centre from both sides. Herodotus gives 6,400 Persian dead against 192 Athenians, figures usually treated as approximate at best.

The Persian fleet then sailed for Athens itself, and the Athenian army marched back the same day to find the city defended. The modern marathon race commemorates a later legend; the run Herodotus actually describes is that of Pheidippides, sent some 240 km to Sparta to ask for help before the battle.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marathon).

layers.label: The army marched back to Athens the same day
Pheidippides was sent some 240 km to Sparta to ask for help

name: Battle of Thermopylae
summary: A small Greek force held the coastal pass against Xerxes' army for two days of fighting before a mountain path let the Persians round behind it.
body:
Part of [Greco-Persian Wars](event:greco-persian-wars). The Battle of Thermopylae was fought over three days in August or September 480 BCE at a narrow pass between the mountains and the sea in central Greece, where a Greek force under Leonidas I of Sparta blocked the advance of Xerxes' army.

The Greek plan was to hold the pass while the fleet held the strait at Artemisium alongside it, denying the Persians both routes south at once. Roughly seven thousand Greeks from several states took the position. The size of the Persian army is not recoverable: Herodotus writes of over two million men, and modern estimates run from about seventy thousand to a few hundred thousand.

The narrow ground cancelled the Persian advantage in numbers, and the Greeks held two days of assaults, including one by the king's own guard. A local man, Ephialtes, then showed the Persians a mountain track that came out behind the pass. Warned that he was being encircled, Leonidas sent most of the army away and stayed with about three hundred Spartans, seven hundred Thespians and four hundred Thebans. All were killed.

The delay was short and the Greek fleet withdrew from Artemisium at the same time, leaving Attica to be evacuated and Athens burned. The stand was commemorated at once (Simonides' epitaph for the Spartan dead is quoted by Herodotus) and has been retold as an emblem of resistance against odds ever since.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Thermopylae).

layers.label: Xerxes' army came down from Thessaly
A mountain track came out behind the pass

name: Battle of Salamis
summary: The Greek fleet destroyed the larger Persian navy in the narrows off Salamis, forcing Xerxes to withdraw.
body:
Part of [Greco-Persian Wars](event:greco-persian-wars). The Battle of Salamis was fought in September 480 BCE in the strait between the island of Salamis and the coast of Attica. The allied Greek fleet defeated the larger Persian fleet, and Xerxes withdrew to Asia with much of his army.

Athens had been evacuated to Salamis and the Aegean islands after the pass at Thermopylae fell, and the city was burned. The allied commanders argued over whether to fall back to the Isthmus of Corinth. Themistocles, who had persuaded Athens to spend the silver of the Laurium mines on a fleet in the 480s, argued for fighting in the strait, where numbers would not tell, and, according to Herodotus, sent a false message to Xerxes that the Greeks were about to scatter, to make sure the Persians attacked.

The Persian fleet entered the narrows at night and fought in confusion the next day in cramped water, its ships colliding as the Greek triremes rammed. Losses were heavy and one-sided. Xerxes watched from a throne on the shore, and left for Asia with part of the army, leaving Mardonius in Greece with the rest.

The victory ended the threat to the Peloponnese by sea and made the following year's land campaign winnable. Aeschylus, who probably fought in the battle, staged it in *The Persians* eight years later, the earliest surviving European play about a historical event.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Salamis).

name: Roman law developed and codified
summary: A system of jurisprudence emerged over centuries, from the Twelve Tables to Justinian's Digest, and became the basis of the civil law tradition.
body:
Roman law developed over roughly a thousand years, from the Twelve Tables of about 450 BCE to the codification ordered by [Justinian](event:justinian) in the sixth century CE. It is the foundation of the civil law systems used today across Europe, Latin America and much of Asia and Africa.

The Twelve Tables were the first written statement of Roman law, published on bronze in the Forum after plebeian agitation against judgments nobody could check. What grew from them was less a code than a practice. Each year the praetor published an edict setting out the actions he would allow, and the edict was extended by his successors; jurists (private specialists, not officials) gave opinions on cases, and their reasoning, not statute, is where most of the law was made. Gaius' *Institutes*, a textbook of about 161 CE, is the only work of classical jurisprudence to survive nearly whole.

The Romans distinguished public law from private, and within private law worked out the categories still in use: persons, things and actions; ownership and possession; contract, delict, inheritance; legal personality; and the *ius gentium*, the law held to apply to everyone rather than to citizens only.

Justinian's commission compiled the whole into the *Corpus Juris Civilis* between 529 and 534, of which the *Digest* is a distillation of the jurists. Rediscovered and taught at Bologna from the late eleventh century, it was received into the law of most of continental Europe and carried from there around the world.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_law).

name: Parthenon built
summary: Athens crowned its Acropolis with a marble temple to Athena, paid for out of the tribute of its empire.
body:
Part of [Athenian democracy](event:athenian-democracy). The Parthenon is the temple of Athena Parthenos on the Acropolis of Athens, built between 447 and 432 BCE at the height of the city's power. It is the best-known surviving building of classical Greece.

It replaced an earlier temple destroyed by the Persians in 480 BCE, and was paid for largely out of the tribute of the Delian League, the alliance Athens led and by then controlled. The league's treasury had been moved from Delos to Athens in 454. The architects were Iktinos and Kallikrates; Phidias directed the sculpture.

The building is Doric, eight columns by seventeen, with Ionic features inside, and is built almost entirely of marble from Mount Pentelicus. Its horizontal lines curve slightly upward and its columns lean inward and swell at the middle, refinements usually explained as optical corrections. The sculptural programme (the pediments, the metopes and a continuous frieze running round the inner chamber, most probably showing the Panathenaic procession) was unusually extensive. Inside stood Phidias' statue of Athena, some twelve metres high, in gold and ivory.

The temple served as a church and later a mosque, which is why it stood almost intact until 1687, when Venetian artillery hit the Ottoman powder store inside it and blew out the centre. Much of the surviving sculpture was removed by Lord Elgin between 1801 and 1812 and is in the British Museum, which Greece continues to contest.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenon).

name: Herodotus writes the Histories
summary: Herodotus, later called the "Father of History", wrote the first extended prose enquiry into the past, centred on the Greco-Persian Wars.
body:
Herodotus of Halicarnassus, who lived from about 484 to about 425 BCE, wrote the *Histories*, an account of the [Greco-Persian Wars](event:greco-persian-wars) and of the peoples the Persians ruled. Cicero called him the father of history, and the work is the earliest surviving Greek prose narrative of any length.

His first word, *historíē*, means enquiry, and he states his purpose at the outset: to preserve what men have done from being forgotten, and to explain why Greeks and barbarians came to fight. He travelled widely (Egypt, the Levant, Mesopotamia, the Black Sea coast), questioned informants, compared their accounts, and frequently reports two versions of a story without deciding between them.

The nine books, named after the Muses by later editors, begin with the rise of Lydia and Persia and end with the Greek counter-offensive of 479 BCE. Long digressions describe Egyptian religion, Scythian burial customs, Babylonian building and Indian gold. He includes oracles, dreams and marvels, which is why Plutarch and others called him a liar; archaeology and Egyptology have confirmed a good deal that was once dismissed, and disproved some of the rest.

Thucydides, writing a generation later about the [Peloponnesian War](event:peloponnesian-war), deliberately narrowed the subject to politics and war and excluded the marvellous. The two together set the range within which later history was written.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herodotus).

name: Peloponnesian War
summary: Athens and Sparta fought for twenty-seven years; Athens lost its fleet, its empire and, for a time, its democracy.
body:
The Peloponnesian War was fought between Athens and its empire and the Spartan-led Peloponnesian League from 431 to 404 BCE. Sparta won. Athens surrendered its fleet, its walls and its overseas possessions.

Thucydides, an Athenian general exiled during the war, wrote its history and named its cause: the growth of Athenian power and the fear this produced in Sparta. The immediate quarrels were about allies and trade (Corcyra, Potidaea, a decree excluding Megara from Athenian markets), and the two sides were mismatched. Athens had the fleet, the tribute of the Delian League and walls that ran down to its port; Sparta had the best infantry in Greece and could march into Attica at will but could not take the city.

Pericles' strategy was to abandon the countryside, live on imported grain and use the fleet to raid. A plague in the crowded city killed perhaps a quarter of the population, Pericles among them, in the war's second and third years. The later phases turned on Sicily and then on the Aegean, where Persian money finally gave Sparta a fleet that could beat the Athenian one.

The war brought sieges, massacres and civil war within cities into Greek practice, and Thucydides' account of them, the Melian dialogue above all, is read as the founding text of realist political analysis. Sparta's own hegemony lasted barely thirty years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peloponnesian_War).

steps.name: The Archidamian War
steps.page: Sparta invaded Attica each summer and burned the crops; the Athenians retreated behind the Long Walls and raided the Peloponnesian coast from the sea. Neither could reach the other's strength. The fighting ran on for ten years through Pylos, Sphacteria and the loss of Amphipolis, where both Cleon and the Spartan Brasidas were killed.

steps.name: The plague at Athens
steps.page: An epidemic entered the crowded city through the Piraeus in 430 BCE and returned twice more. It killed perhaps a quarter to a third of the population, including Pericles in 429. Thucydides caught it, survived, and described the symptoms and the collapse of civic order in the clinical detail that made his account a model for later writers on plague.

steps.name: The Peace of Nicias
steps.page: A treaty in 421 BCE was meant to restore what each side had taken and to hold for fifty years. It held for six, in name only. Neither Corinth nor Thebes accepted it, prisoners and places went unreturned, and Athens and Sparta fought each other through allies, most openly at Mantinea in 418 BCE.

steps.name: The Sicilian Expedition
steps.page: Athens sent a fleet to Sicily in 415 BCE, invited by a minor ally against Syracuse and hoping to take the island's resources. Alcibiades, one of its three commanders, was recalled to face a charge of sacrilege and defected to Sparta. The siege of Syracuse failed; a relief fleet was destroyed in the harbour, and the retreating army was cut off and enslaved. Athens lost some two hundred ships and tens of thousands of men.

steps.name: The Ionian War
steps.page: Sparta fortified Decelea inside Attica, which cost Athens its silver mines and its farmland year-round, and took Persian subsidies in exchange for conceding the Greek cities of Asia. The war moved to the Aegean, where Athens rebuilt fleets and won at Cynossema and Arginusae, and where its democracy was overthrown in 411 and restored a year later.

steps.name: Aegospotami
steps.page: Lysander caught the Athenian fleet beached and unprepared on the Hellespont in 405 BCE and took almost all of it. With the straits in Spartan hands the grain route from the Black Sea was cut, and Athens could neither feed itself nor put another fleet to sea.

steps.name: The surrender of Athens
steps.page: Athens capitulated in the spring of 404 BCE after a winter of blockade and hunger. The Long Walls were pulled down, the fleet reduced to a dozen ships, and the empire dissolved. A Spartan-backed oligarchy of thirty ruled for a year and killed some fifteen hundred citizens; democracy was restored in 403, and Socrates was tried four years later.

name: Maya calendar systems
summary: The Maya ran interlocking cycles of 260 and 365 days alongside a Long Count that numbered every day from a fixed starting point.
body:
The Maya kept several calendars at once and read dates from the combination of them. Two cycles turned continuously (the 260-day *tzolk'in* and the 365-day *haab'*), and a separate Long Count numbered days in an unbroken sequence from a fixed starting point, which let a date be written without ambiguity across thousands of years.

The tzolk'in pairs thirteen numbers with twenty day names, giving 260 unique days, and governed ritual and divination. The haab' has eighteen months of twenty days plus a five-day remainder considered unlucky. Because the two run together, a given pairing recurs only once in 18,980 days, the 52-year Calendar Round, which is common to Mesoamerica.

The Long Count counts days, then units of 20 days, 360 days, 7,200 days and 144,000 days, and its zero point falls on 11 August 3114 BCE in the correlation most scholars accept. It is not exclusively Maya: the earliest surviving Long Count dates are from Chiapas and the Gulf coast in the first century BCE, before the [Classic Maya](event:maya-classic) cities. It was used above all on monuments, to fix the reigns and deeds of rulers.

The same arithmetic supported astronomy. The Dresden Codex, one of four Maya books to survive the Spanish conquest, contains tables tracking the 584-day cycle of Venus and predicting the seasons in which eclipses could occur.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesoamerican_Long_Count_calendar).

name: Trial and death of Socrates
summary: Athens condemned Socrates to drink hemlock for impiety and corrupting the young.
body:
In 399 BCE an Athenian court tried Socrates on charges of impiety: of not recognising the gods the city recognised, of introducing new divinities, and of corrupting the young. He was convicted and sentenced to death, and drank hemlock in prison.

Socrates wrote nothing. He is known through the dialogues of his pupil Plato, the memoirs of Xenophon, and a caricature in Aristophanes' *Clouds*. He questioned Athenians about justice, courage and piety, showed that their confident answers contradicted themselves, and claimed no knowledge of his own beyond knowing that he did not know. The Delphic oracle, he said, had called no one wiser.

The charges were brought by Meletus, Anytus and Lycon before a jury of some five hundred citizens. The political background mattered: Athens had lost the [Peloponnesian War](event:peloponnesian-war) five years earlier and endured the rule of the Thirty, several of whom had been in Socrates' circle, and an amnesty barred prosecution for those years directly. Plato's *Apology* has him refuse to plead for mercy and propose, as his penalty, free meals at public expense; the jury then voted for death by a wider margin than it had voted to convict. He declined an offer to escape.

His method of argument passed through Plato and [Aristotle](event:aristotle) into later Western philosophy.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_Socrates).

name: Plato founds the Academy
summary: Plato opened a school in a grove outside Athens that taught mathematics, dialectic and philosophy and became a model for later institutions of learning.
body:
Plato founded a school about 387 BCE in a grove sacred to the hero Academus, outside the walls of Athens. It taught for most of the next three centuries and gave every later academy its name.

It was not a school in the modern sense: there were no fees, no fixed curriculum and no degrees, but a community of members who lived and argued together. Mathematics was central (a later tradition put 'let no one ignorant of geometry enter' over the door), because Plato held that abstract, unchanging objects are what knowledge is really of, and that geometry trains the mind to grasp them. The method was dialectic, argument by question and answer, and the written dialogues that survive are the public face of it. [Aristotle](event:aristotle) studied there for twenty years before leaving to found his own school.

Its doctrines changed sharply after Plato. Under Arcesilaus in the third century BCE and Carneades in the second, the Academy turned sceptical, arguing against every position rather than defending any, which is close to the opposite of what its founder taught.

The buildings were destroyed when Sulla besieged Athens in 86 BCE. Platonism continued to be taught at Athens, and a Neoplatonic school there was closed by an edict of Justinian in 529 CE; whether that school was in any real sense the same institution is disputed.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plato's_Academy).

name: Aristotle
summary: Aristotle systematised logic, biology, physics, ethics and politics, and tutored the young Alexander.
body:
Aristotle, who lived from 384 to 322 BCE, was a Greek philosopher whose work covers logic, physics, biology, psychology, metaphysics, ethics, politics, rhetoric and poetics. He founded the discipline of logic, did the first systematic biology, and shaped European and Islamic learning for nearly two thousand years.

Born at Stagira in northern Greece, the son of a doctor, he came to Athens at seventeen and spent twenty years in [Plato's Academy](event:plato-academy). After Plato's death he worked in Asia Minor and on Lesbos, where he dissected and described marine animals, and from about 343 BCE he tutored the young [Alexander](event:alexander-conquests) at the Macedonian court. He returned to Athens in 335 and taught at the Lyceum; his followers were called Peripatetics.

He rejected Plato's separate realm of Forms and looked for the form of a thing in the thing itself. He explained change through four kinds of cause (material, formal, efficient and final), held that everything in nature has a characteristic function, and built an ethics on that idea: the good life is the exercise of reason and virtue, learned as a habit, aiming at *eudaimonia*. His syllogistic remained the whole of formal logic until the nineteenth century.

What survives is mostly lecture material rather than published work. Translated into Arabic and then Latin, it became the framework of medieval [scholastic](event:scholasticism) philosophy, in which he was cited simply as 'the Philosopher', and his physics and cosmology held until [Copernicus](event:copernicus) and Galileo.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle).

name: Conquests of Alexander the Great
summary: In eleven years Alexander of Macedon destroyed the Persian Empire and led an army from Greece to the Punjab.
body:
Alexander III of Macedon crossed into Asia in 334 BCE and by 330 had destroyed the [Achaemenid Empire](event:achaemenid-empire), the largest state of its day. He campaigned for another seven years, as far as the Punjab, and died at Babylon in 323 BCE at the age of thirty-two, having never lost a battle.

He inherited the plan and the army from his father Philip II, who had made Macedon the dominant power in Greece and drilled an infantry armed with the long *sarissa* pike, supported by heavy Companion cavalry. Alexander's method was consistent: pin the enemy line with the phalanx, find or force a gap, and drive the cavalry through it at the enemy commander. Three victories (the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela) broke Persian field armies, and sieges of Tyre and Gaza showed that fortified cities would not hold him either.

He was crowned in Egypt, burned the palace at Persepolis, took the Persian royal title and much of the Persian administration with it, married the Bactrian Roxana, ordered mass marriages between his officers and Iranian women, and kept satraps in place, policies that his Macedonians resented. His army finally refused to go further east at the Hyphasis.

He left no viable heir. Within a generation his generals had divided the conquests into the Seleucid, Ptolemaic and Antigonid kingdoms. The Greek language, coinage, city plan and civic institutions they carried with them reached from [Egypt](event:alexandria) to Afghanistan.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_Alexander_the_Great).

steps.name: Crossing into Asia: the Granicus
steps.page: Alexander crossed the Hellespont in the spring of 334 BCE with about 40,000 men and met the satraps' army at the river Granicus in May. He attacked across the river at once. The victory opened western Anatolia; he took the Ionian cities and, at Gordium, is said to have cut the knot that was supposed to be untied only by the future ruler of Asia.

steps.name: Issus
steps.page: Darius III brought the royal army round behind Alexander and cut his supply line, forcing a battle on a narrow coastal plain in Cilicia in November 333 BCE where his numbers could not be used. The Persian line broke, Darius fled the field, and his mother, wife and daughters were captured in the camp.

steps.name: The siege of Tyre
steps.page: Rather than pursue Darius, Alexander turned south to take the Phoenician ports and deny the Persian fleet its bases. Tyre, on an island half a kilometre offshore, held out for seven months in 332 BCE until a mole was built out to its walls. Gaza fell after two months more, and Egypt surrendered without a fight.

steps.name: Persepolis and the death of Darius
steps.page: Babylon and Susa surrendered with their treasuries. Alexander forced the Persian Gates in winter and entered Persepolis, whose palace was burned in 330 BCE. Whether that was policy or the result of a drinking party was already argued in antiquity. Darius, a fugitive, was killed by his own satrap Bessus that summer, and Alexander had him buried as a king and took the title himself.

steps.name: Bactria and Sogdiana
steps.page: The eastern satrapies took three years and cost more than the Persian field armies had. Alexander fought a war of forts, raids and reprisals across what is now Afghanistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, founded garrison cities, took the Sogdian Rock, and married Roxana. It was in these years that he killed his officer Cleitus in a quarrel and that a conspiracy among his pages was uncovered.

steps.name: The Hydaspes and the Hyphasis
steps.page: Crossing into the Punjab in 326 BCE, Alexander beat King Porus at the Hydaspes in a monsoon river crossing, his hardest-fought battle and the first against war elephants in numbers. At the next river, the Hyphasis, the army refused to go on. He turned south down the Indus instead of east.

steps.name: The return through Gedrosia
steps.page: From the Indus delta the fleet under Nearchus followed the coast while Alexander marched the army back through the Gedrosian desert in what is now Baluchistan, in the autumn and winter of 325 BCE. Thirst, heat and a flash flood killed a large part of the column and most of the followers with it, the worst losses of the whole expedition and the only ones not inflicted by an enemy.

steps.name: Death at Babylon
steps.page: Alexander returned to Babylon and was planning an expedition into Arabia when he fell ill after a long banquet and died eleven days later, in June 323 BCE, aged thirty-two. Fever, poison and heavy drinking have all been proposed. Asked who should succeed him, he is reported to have said 'the strongest'; his generals fought over the answer for forty years.

name: Battle of Gaugamela
summary: Alexander broke the main Persian army under Darius III, opening Mesopotamia and Persia to conquest.
body:
Part of [Conquests of Alexander the Great](event:alexander-conquests). The Battle of Gaugamela was fought on 1 October 331 BCE on a plain in northern Mesopotamia, near modern Mosul. Alexander destroyed the main army of the Persian Empire, and Darius III never fielded another.

Darius had chosen the ground and had it levelled so that his scythed chariots and cavalry could be used, and had drawn troops from the eastern satrapies as far as Bactria and India. The Persian force was much the larger. Ancient writers give figures in the hundreds of thousands or a million; modern estimates run between fifty and a hundred and twenty thousand, against about 47,000 with Alexander.

Alexander advanced obliquely to his right, drawing the Persian left out after him and opening a gap in the enemy line. He turned the Companion cavalry into it in a wedge aimed at Darius himself. As at Issus, Darius left the field, and his army followed. The Greek left under Parmenion was meanwhile hard pressed and the camp was plundered, which is why the pursuit was broken off.

Babylon and Susa surrendered with their treasuries within weeks. Darius fled east and was killed by his own satrap the following summer. The battle is conventionally taken as the end of the [Achaemenid Empire](event:achaemenid-empire).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Gaugamela).

name: Founding of Alexandria
summary: Alexander laid out a Greek city on the Egyptian coast that became the leading centre of learning in the Mediterranean.
body:
Part of [Conquests of Alexander the Great](event:alexander-conquests). Alexander founded Alexandria in 331 BCE on the Egyptian coast west of the Nile delta, on the site of a fishing village beside the island of Pharos. It became the capital of Ptolemaic Egypt and, for three centuries, the largest and richest city of the Greek world.

The site had a sheltered double harbour and a canal link to the Nile, which made it the outlet for Egyptian grain and the entrepôt between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea trade with Arabia and India. The city was laid out on a grid, with a causeway running out to Pharos, on which the Ptolemies built a lighthouse over a hundred metres high, counted among the wonders of the ancient world.

Ptolemy I, one of Alexander's generals, took Egypt after his death and brought Alexander's body there. He and his successors funded the Museum, a state-supported research institution, and its [Library](event:library-alexandria), which drew Euclid, Eratosthenes and Aristarchus. The population was mixed: Greek, Egyptian and a large Jewish community, for whom the Hebrew scriptures were translated into Greek here.

It passed to Rome with [Cleopatra's](item:cleopatra-vii) defeat in 30 BCE and remained the empire's second city. Some seventy other cities were named after Alexander; this is the largest and best known.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandria).

name: Mauryan Empire and Ashoka
summary: Chandragupta Maurya unified most of the Indian subcontinent; his grandson Ashoka renounced war for Buddhism.
body:
The Maurya Empire, founded by Chandragupta Maurya about 322 BCE, was the first state to rule most of the Indian subcontinent. Under his grandson Ashoka it reached from Afghanistan to Bengal and south almost to the tip of the peninsula.

Chandragupta overthrew the Nanda dynasty of Magadha and took its capital, Pataliputra on the Ganges, reportedly with the guidance of the minister Kautilya, to whom the *Arthashastra* (a manual of statecraft, taxation and espionage) is attributed. He then drove Alexander's successor Seleucus out of the Indus provinces and concluded a treaty about 303 BCE, ceding him five hundred war elephants in exchange for territory and a marriage alliance. The Greek ambassador Megasthenes left a description of Pataliputra and its administration.

Ashoka, who ruled from about 268 to 232 BCE, conquered Kalinga on the east coast in a campaign whose slaughter he afterwards said he regretted. He turned to [Buddhism](event:buddha), and had edicts carved on rock faces and polished sandstone pillars across the empire (in local Prakrit, and in Greek and Aramaic at Kandahar), proclaiming *dhamma*: non-violence, respect for all religious traditions, care for the sick and for animals, and the planting of wells and shade trees along roads. He sent missions to Sri Lanka and to the Hellenistic kings of the west.

The empire broke up after his death and ended in 185 BCE. The lion capital of his pillar at Sarnath is the state emblem of the Republic of India.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurya_Empire).

name: Roman road network expands
summary: Rome laid some 400,000 km of roads, about 80,000 km of them paved, used for armies, trade and the official post.
body:
Part of [Roman Republic formally established](event:roman-republic-founded). The Romans built a road network that eventually ran to some 400,000 km, of which about 80,000 km were paved with stone. It was laid out to move armies, and everything else in the empire moved along it afterwards.

The Via Appia, begun in 312 BCE by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus to carry troops south towards Capua, set the pattern. A surveyed line was taken as straight as the ground allowed, with cuttings, embankments and bridges rather than detours; the roadbed was dug out and built up in layers of packed stone, gravel and mortar, cambered so that water ran off into side ditches, and topped with fitted paving blocks on the main routes. Milestones gave the distance to the nearest town, and from Augustus onward a golden milestone in the Forum was the notional origin of them all.

Roads were named after the magistrate who commissioned them and maintained by the state. A legion could cover about 30 km a day on one; the imperial courier service, the *cursus publicus*, with relays of horses at posting stations, moved messages far faster. Trade, tax collection, [pilgrimage and mission](event:spread-christianity) followed.

Many survive as the alignment of modern roads, and a few (stretches of the Appia, bridges in Spain and Turkey) are still usable. Nothing comparable was built in Europe again until the eighteenth century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_roads).

name: Epicureanism emerges
summary: Epicurus taught that pleasure, defined as the absence of pain, is the good, and that simple life brings more pleasure than excess.
body:
Epicurus founded a school in Athens about 306 BCE, in a house with a garden that gave the community its name. He taught that pleasure is the only thing good in itself, and that the pleasure worth having is the absence of bodily pain and mental disturbance.

The physics is atomism, taken from Democritus and modified: the universe consists of atoms falling through void, with an unpredictable swerve that leaves room for free will. It is not designed and not governed. The gods exist but are untroubled and take no interest in human affairs, so there is nothing to fear from them; and since the soul is made of atoms that disperse at death, there is no one left to suffer, so 'death is nothing to us'. The purpose of the physics is to remove those two fears.

The ethics that follows is modest rather than indulgent. Desires that are natural and necessary (food, shelter, company) are easily satisfied; desires for wealth, fame and power are not, and cause the trouble they promise to cure. Friendship, philosophy and plain living produce more pleasure than luxury does. The Garden admitted women and slaves, which was unusual, and Epicureans generally kept out of politics.

The school's later reputation for gluttony comes from hostile critics rather than from its teaching. Its fullest surviving statement is the Latin poem *On the Nature of Things* by Lucretius, recovered in 1417, which fed directly into early modern materialism.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epicureanism).

name: Meroitic script emerges
summary: The Kingdom of Kush developed its own alphabetic script to write the Meroitic language instead of Egyptian.
body:
Part of [Kingdom of Kush rises in Nubia](event:nubian-kush). Meroitic is the script the [Kingdom of Kush](event:nubian-kush) developed to write its own language, in place of the Egyptian hieroglyphs its rulers had used for centuries. The earliest inscriptions date from the third century BCE.

There are two forms. A cursive script, derived from Egyptian demotic, is the older and by far the commoner: about nine in ten surviving texts are written in it. A hieroglyphic form, its signs borrowed in shape from Egyptian, was reserved for monuments and appears a century or more later. Unlike Egyptian, the system is alphasyllabic (twenty-three signs, fifteen consonants carrying an inherent vowel, four separate vowel signs and four syllabic signs), with two or three dots used as word dividers. Cursive text runs right to left.

Francis Llewellyn Griffith worked out the sound values in 1909, largely from Meroitic spellings of names also known in Egyptian. The signs can therefore be read aloud, but the language behind them cannot be understood: it has no established relatives, and the surviving corpus is small and mostly funerary and formulaic, so vocabulary cannot be recovered from context. A few dozen words are known with confidence.

Meroitic is one of the earliest written African languages south of Egypt, and remains among the few ancient scripts that can be pronounced but not translated. It went out of use with the fall of Meroë in the fourth century CE.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meroitic_script).

name: Roman concrete development
summary: Romans mixed lime, volcanic ash and seawater into a durable material that hardened underwater.
body:
Roman concrete, *opus caementicium*, was a mixture of lime mortar, volcanic ash and lumps of aggregate, used from about the third century BCE onward. It let Roman builders shape architecture in mass rather than assemble it from cut blocks, and it is the reason vaults, domes and harbours on the Roman scale were possible.

The essential ingredient was pozzolana, the volcanic ash of the bay of Naples, which reacts with lime to set into a hard, water-resistant mass. Concrete was laid in courses inside timber shuttering or between facings of brick or small stone, so the finished wall looks like masonry and is not. Lighter aggregates could be used where weight mattered: the dome of the [Pantheon](event:pantheon-built) is graded from heavy basalt at the base to porous pumice at the crown, and is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

Its marine version was poured into wooden forms under water for the moles and breakwaters of harbours such as Caesarea. Cores drilled from these have shown that seawater keeps reacting with the ash to grow interlocking crystals, so the concrete gains strength over centuries instead of decaying. Analysis of lime clasts in Roman samples suggests the mixes were made hot and quicklime added directly, giving the material some capacity to seal its own cracks.

The technique was largely lost in the west after the empire and was not matched until modern cements were developed in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_concrete).

name: Stoic philosophy founded
summary: Zeno of Citium taught that virtue is the highest good and that passion should be controlled by reason.
body:
Zeno of Citium began teaching in Athens about 300 BCE in the painted colonnade (the *stoa poikile*) that gave the school its name. Stoicism held that virtue is the only good, that everything else is at best preferable, and that a life goes well when it is lived in accordance with reason and with nature.

The system has three parts. Its physics is materialist and deterministic: the world is a single organism pervaded by a rational principle, the *logos*, and everything that happens follows from what has gone before. Its logic is a formal propositional system, developed chiefly by Chrysippus, more powerful in some respects than Aristotle's. Its ethics follows from both. If events are not in our power but our judgments about them are, then health, wealth, reputation and life itself are not what makes a person good or bad. The destructive emotions are treated as mistaken judgments and can therefore be corrected.

The Roman period supplies almost all the surviving texts: Seneca, a wealthy statesman and Nero's tutor; Epictetus, born a slave, whose lectures were written down by a pupil; and the emperor [Marcus Aurelius](event:marcus-aurelius), writing privately to himself on campaign.

Stoic vocabulary passed into Christian moral theology and into ordinary English, where 'stoical' has narrowed to mean bearing pain without complaint. Its account of judgment and emotion is an acknowledged ancestor of modern cognitive behavioural therapy.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoicism).

name: Library of Alexandria
summary: The Ptolemies assembled the largest collection of scrolls in the ancient world and paid scholars to work on them.
body:
Part of [Founding of Alexandria](event:alexandria). The Library of Alexandria was founded in the early third century BCE by the first Ptolemies as part of the Mouseion, a state-funded institution where scholars were housed, fed and paid to work. It was the largest collection of texts in the ancient Mediterranean.

Its purpose was to hold everything written in Greek, and it was stocked aggressively: agents bought books abroad, and ships putting into the harbour are said to have had their scrolls copied, with the library keeping the originals. Estimates of its size range from forty thousand to several hundred thousand rolls, and no ancient figure is reliable. A branch collection was housed at the temple of Serapis.

The work done there founded textual scholarship. Zenodotus and later Aristarchus produced critical editions of Homer, marking suspect lines; Callimachus compiled the *Pinakes*, a 120-book catalogue of Greek literature that is the ancestor of the library catalogue. Eratosthenes, its third head librarian, measured the circumference of the Earth to within a few per cent using shadow angles at Syene and Alexandria. Euclid and, later, Ptolemy the astronomer worked in the same milieu.

It declined over centuries rather than perishing in one fire. Scholars were expelled in a dynastic purge in 145 BCE, a fire during Caesar's campaign in 48 BCE burned part of the collection, and the palace quarter was destroyed in the fighting of the 270s CE. The Serapeum was demolished in 391.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Alexandria).

name: Punic Wars
summary: Three wars between Rome and Carthage, fought over 118 years, decided who would rule the western Mediterranean.
body:
The Punic Wars were fought between Rome and [Carthage](event:carthage-founding) between 264 and 146 BCE. Rome won all three. The last ended with Carthage destroyed and its territory annexed, and left Rome without a rival anywhere in the western Mediterranean.

The two powers were built differently. Carthage was a maritime and commercial republic with the better navy, a wealthy African hinterland, and armies made up largely of mercenaries and allied contingents. Rome had a citizen militia backed by a network of Italian allies obliged to supply troops, which gave it a manpower reserve deeper than any single defeat could exhaust, the fact that decided the second war.

The first was fought mostly in and around Sicily and turned into a naval contest that Rome, with no naval tradition, entered by building fleets from scratch and losing several of them to storms. The second was Hannibal's: he took the war into Italy and won three annihilating victories there, and still could not make Rome negotiate. The third was brief and one-sided.

The wars also changed Rome. Sicily, Sardinia, Spain and Africa became provinces governed for revenue; the long campaigns produced armies loyal to their commanders and estates worked by enslaved captives; and the small farmers who had filled the legions were displaced. Those strains contributed to the crisis that ended the [Republic](event:roman-republic-fall) a century later.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars).

steps.name: The First Punic War
steps.page: A dispute over Messana drew both powers into Sicily in 264 BCE. Rome built its first war fleets, fitted them with the corvus boarding bridge to turn sea fights into infantry fights, and won at Mylae and Ecnomus while losing hundreds of ships to storms. An invasion of Africa failed. The war ended in 241 BCE with a Roman naval victory off the Aegates Islands, a large indemnity, and Sicily as Rome's first province.

steps.name: Carthage rebuilds in Spain
steps.page: Carthage put down a revolt of its unpaid mercenaries, lost Sardinia and Corsica to Roman opportunism, and turned to Iberia. Hamilcar Barca and then his son-in-law Hasdrubal built a territorial empire on Spanish silver, with a new capital at Carthago Nova. A treaty fixed the Ebro as the limit of Carthaginian expansion; Hannibal's siege of Rome's ally Saguntum in 219 BCE brought the second war.

steps.name: Hannibal crosses the Alps
steps.page: Rather than wait to be invaded, Hannibal marched from Spain in 218 BCE with an army and war elephants, crossed the Rhône and then an Alpine pass in autumn, losing much of his force to the crossing and to hostile tribes. He arrived in the Po valley with perhaps 20,000 infantry and 6,000 cavalry, recruited among the Gauls, and destroyed a Roman army at the Trebia before winter.

steps.name: Lake Trasimene
steps.page: Hannibal drew the consul Flaminius into a march along the northern shore of Lake Trasimene in June 217 BCE and ambushed the column in morning mist between the water and the hills. Some 15,000 Romans were killed, Flaminius among them. Rome appointed Fabius Maximus dictator, who refused battle and shadowed Hannibal instead, a strategy that saved the state and cost him his popularity.

steps.name: The Metaurus
steps.page: Hannibal stayed in Italy for fifteen years without reinforcement, while Rome avoided pitched battles and took Spain and Syracuse instead. When his brother Hasdrubal finally brought an army over the Alps in 207 BCE, an intercepted message let two Roman armies combine and destroy it at the Metaurus. Hannibal is said to have learned of it when his brother's head was thrown into his camp.

steps.name: The Third Punic War
steps.page: Carthage recovered commercially under the peace terms, and when it defended itself against its Numidian neighbour without Roman permission, Rome declared war in 149 BCE. Cato had been ending his speeches with the demand that Carthage be destroyed. The city held out for three years, was stormed street by street in the spring of 146 BCE, and was razed; the survivors were enslaved and the territory became the province of Africa.

name: Qin unification of China
summary: Ying Zheng conquered the six rival states, declared himself First Emperor, and imposed one script, one currency and one law on China.
body:
Between 230 and 221 BCE the state of Qin conquered the six kingdoms that had divided China since the [Zhou](event:zhou-dynasty) court lost control of them, and its king Ying Zheng took the new title Shi Huangdi, First Emperor. The dynasty he founded lasted fifteen years; the unified empire it created has been restored again and again ever since.

Qin's advantage was a century of Legalist reform. Beginning with Shang Yang in the fourth century BCE, it had replaced hereditary privilege with promotion by military merit, registered its population in mutually liable households, taxed land directly and codified harsh, uniformly applied law. It could therefore raise, feed and move armies its neighbours could not match.

After the conquest, the aristocracies of the defeated states were moved to the capital and their walls pulled down. The empire was divided into commanderies and counties run by appointed officials rather than by hereditary lords, the framework of Chinese administration for the next two thousand years. Weights, measures, coinage, the width of cart axles and the writing system were standardised, and the small seal script imposed on all of them.

The same methods drew lasting criticism. Books held to encourage criticism of the present by appeal to the past were ordered burned, scholars were executed, and hundreds of thousands were conscripted for the [Great Wall](event:great-wall), the road network and the emperor's [tomb](event:terracotta-army). The First Emperor died in 210 BCE while touring the east, and rebellion brought the dynasty down within four years, leaving the [Han](event:han-dynasty) to inherit the machinery he had built.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin_dynasty).

steps.name: The conquest of the six states
steps.page: Qin took Han in 230 BCE, Zhao in 228, Wei in 225, Chu (the largest and hardest, needing an army said to be 600,000 strong) in 223, Yan in 222 and Qi, which surrendered without a fight, in 221. Nine years ended more than five centuries of warfare between the Chinese states.

steps.name: Ying Zheng becomes the First Emperor
steps.page: In 221 BCE Ying Zheng judged the old title of king inadequate and coined a new one, huangdi, joining the words for the mythical sovereigns and thearchs: Shi Huangdi, First Emperor, with his successors to be numbered after him. The empire was divided into thirty-six commanderies under appointed governors, and the capital fixed at Xianyang.

steps.name: One script, one coin, one axle
steps.page: The chancellor Li Si oversaw the standardisation of the writing system on a simplified seal script, of weights and measures, and of currency on a round bronze coin with a square hole that outlasted every dynasty that issued it. Cart axles were fixed to a single width so that wheels would run in the ruts of the new imperial roads, and the noble families of the conquered states were resettled at the capital.

steps.name: The burning of the books
steps.page: On Li Si's proposal in 213 BCE, private copies of the classics, of poetry and of the histories of the conquered states were ordered surrendered and burned; manuals of medicine, divination and agriculture were exempt, and copies were kept in the imperial archive. Tradition adds the burial alive of scholars the following year. Later Confucian historians treated the episode as the defining crime of the dynasty, and modern scholars regard their account as coloured by it.

steps.name: Rebellion and the fall of Qin
steps.page: The First Emperor died on tour in 210 BCE; his death was concealed until the succession could be fixed on a compliant younger son. Within a year conscripts who would have been executed for arriving late rose in revolt, and the old aristocracies rose with them. Xianyang fell in 206 BCE. Liu Bang, a village official turned rebel, beat his rival Xiang Yu and founded the [Han](event:han-dynasty) in 202.

name: Great Wall of China
summary: Frontier walls were linked and repeatedly rebuilt over eighteen centuries; most of what survives is Ming work.
body:
Part of [Qin unification of China](event:qin-unification). The Great Wall is not one wall but a series of fortifications built, rebuilt and abandoned along China's northern frontier over some eighteen centuries. Surveys that count every branch and period put the total at about 21,000 km.

Rival states were already walling their northern borders before unification. After 221 BCE the Qin general Meng Tian was sent north with a large army and a conscripted workforce to link and extend these lines against the Xiongnu; almost nothing of that wall survives, since it was rammed earth. The [Han](event:han-dynasty) pushed a wall of their own far west into the Gansu corridor to protect the [Silk Road](event:silk-road) trade. Later dynasties, particularly those of northern origin, saw little use for it and let it decay.

What visitors see today is Ming work, built between the fourteenth and seventeenth centuries after the Mongols were driven out and rebuilt in brick and dressed stone, with watchtowers, garrison forts and beacon towers that could pass a signal along the line faster than a rider. It ran about 8,850 km.

As a barrier it worked when it was garrisoned and failed when it was not: the Ming wall did not stop the Manchu conquest of 1644, which came through a pass opened by a defecting general. It also functioned as a customs line and a control on movement. Contrary to a persistent claim, it is not visible to the naked eye from orbit.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Wall_of_China).

layers.label: The Ming wall, about 8,850 km from Jiayuguan to the sea
The Han wall, pushed far west into the Gansu corridor

name: Battle of Cannae
summary: Hannibal's double envelopment destroyed a much larger Roman army in southern Italy.
body:
Part of [Punic Wars](event:punic-wars). The Battle of Cannae was fought on 2 August 216 BCE in Apulia, in southern Italy, between Hannibal's army and the largest force Rome had ever put in the field. The Roman army was surrounded and destroyed in a single day.

Rome had raised eight legions with allied contingents (perhaps 80,000 men, against Hannibal's 50,000) and put them under the two consuls of the year on alternating days of command. Hannibal drew his centre up in a shallow curve bulging towards the enemy, with his weaker Spanish and Gallic infantry there and his best African troops in column on the flanks.

The Roman infantry pushed the centre back, as it was meant to, until the curve reversed and the legions were pressing into a pocket. The African columns then turned inwards on both sides while Hannibal's cavalry, having beaten the Roman horse on both wings, came round behind. The Romans were compressed until they could not use their weapons. Polybius puts the dead at around 48,000; Livy at 55,000, with the consul Aemilius Paullus and eighty senators among them.

Rome refused to negotiate, raised new legions and returned to Fabius' strategy of avoiding battle. Several southern cities and Syracuse changed sides, but the Italian allies mostly held. Cannae remains the standard textbook example of double envelopment.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cannae).

name: Terracotta Army
summary: Some 8,000 life-sized clay soldiers were buried to guard the first emperor's tomb; farmers rediscovered them in 1974.
body:
Part of [Qin unification of China](event:qin-unification). The Terracotta Army is a collection of life-sized clay figures buried in pits about 1.5 km east of the tomb mound of the First Emperor, near Xi'an, to accompany him after his death in 210 BCE. Farmers digging a well found the first fragments in March 1974.

Three pits have been excavated. The largest holds an estimated 6,000 infantry in battle order in parallel corridors; a second contains cavalry, chariots and archers; a third, much smaller, appears to be a command post. Something over 8,000 warriors, 130 chariots and 670 horses are thought to be present in all, together with pits of bronze waterfowl, acrobats and officials found later.

The figures were mass-produced from moulded parts (legs, torsos, arms, heads) and then finished individually, so that faces, hair and armour differ while the components repeat. They were painted in bright colours, most of which flaked away within minutes of exposure to dry air after excavation. Their weapons were real: bronze swords, crossbow triggers and tens of thousands of arrowheads, made to tolerances that indicate standardised workshops and inspected batches.

The tomb mound itself has not been opened. Sima Qian, writing a century later, described a chamber with a map of the empire and rivers of flowing mercury; soil surveys have found anomalously high mercury concentrations above it.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army).

name: Han dynasty
summary: Four centuries of Han rule set the pattern of Chinese imperial government and gave the majority ethnic group its name.
body:
The Han ruled China from 202 BCE to 220 CE, apart from a fifteen-year interruption. It was the dynasty that made the empire the [Qin](event:qin-unification) had created workable, and it set the pattern of Chinese government for the next two millennia. The majority ethnic group of China still calls itself Han.

Liu Bang, a minor official who rose in the rebellions against the Qin, took the throne as Emperor Gaozu. The early Han kept the Qin machinery of commanderies and appointed officials but abandoned its harshest laws and lowered taxes. Under Emperor Wu, who reigned from 141 to 87 BCE, the state expanded into Central Asia, northern Vietnam and Korea, drove the Xiongnu confederation back beyond the Gobi, established monopolies on salt and iron, and made [Confucian](event:confucius) learning the qualification for office, the beginning of a bureaucracy recruited on education rather than birth, and of an imperial academy to supply it. The mission of Zhang Qian west of the Pamirs opened the [Silk Road](event:silk-road).

The period was inventive: [paper](event:paper-invention), the seismoscope of Zhang Heng, the wheelbarrow, the chain pump, the stern-mounted rudder and blast-furnace cast iron all date from it, as does Sima Qian's *Records of the Grand Historian*, the model for every later dynastic history.

Court factions, the power of consort families and eunuchs, and the concentration of land in great estates weakened it. The Yellow Turban rebellion of 184 CE broke the state's control, and by 220 the empire had split into the Three Kingdoms.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty).

name: Battle of Zama
summary: Scipio Africanus defeated Hannibal in North Africa, ending the Second Punic War.
body:
Part of [Punic Wars](event:punic-wars). The Battle of Zama was fought in October 202 BCE on the plains inland from Carthage. Scipio defeated Hannibal, and the Second Punic War ended.

Scipio had taken the war to Spain and then, against considerable opposition in the Senate, crossed to Africa in 204 BCE. He destroyed two armies in their camps, brought the Numidian prince Masinissa over to Rome with his cavalry (the arm that had won Hannibal his victories in Italy), and forced Carthage to recall Hannibal from Italy after fifteen years there.

Hannibal opened with eighty war elephants. Scipio had drawn his maniples up in columns with lanes between them and met the charge with trumpets and javelins, so that most of the elephants ran down the lanes or back through their own lines. The infantry then fought to a standstill until the Roman and Numidian cavalry, which had chased the Carthaginian horse off the field, returned and struck the rear.

The peace stripped Carthage of Spain and of all territory outside Africa, cut its navy to ten ships, imposed an indemnity of 10,000 talents over fifty years, and forbade it to wage war without Rome's consent, the clause that produced the third war half a century later. Scipio took the name Africanus; Hannibal went into exile and eventually took poison.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama).

name: Fall of the Roman Republic
summary: A century of political violence and civil war destroyed the republican constitution and left one man in charge of the Roman world.
body:
The Roman Republic did not end on a single day. Between the killing of the tribune Tiberius Gracchus in 133 BCE and the settlement of 27 BCE, in which the Senate handed Octavian a permanent extraordinary position and the name Augustus, the constitution was overwhelmed by problems it had no procedure for and by men who had armies.

Conquest had made the Republic rich and unmanageable. Provinces were governed for a year at a time by magistrates who had bought their way to office and expected to recoup the cost; the small farmers who had filled the legions were displaced by great estates worked by enslaved captives; and after Marius the army was recruited from the landless and looked to its general, not the Senate, for its discharge and its land. Once Sulla marched on Rome in 88 BCE, an army in Italy was a political instrument.

Politics polarised into those who worked through the popular assemblies and those who defended the Senate's authority, and the argument was increasingly settled by riot, murder and proscription. Three men in turn (Sulla, Caesar, Octavian) held the state by force and had the constitution declare it legal.

Augustus kept every republican form: the Senate met, consuls were elected, and he called himself first citizen. In practice he kept control of the armies, the treasury and appointments. The result, the [Empire](event:roman-empire), was stable for two centuries and was never again a republic.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_of_the_Roman_Republic).

steps.name: The Gracchi
steps.page: Tiberius Gracchus, tribune in 133 BCE, put a land redistribution bill to the people over the Senate's objection and was beaten to death by senators and their clients. His brother Gaius pushed further reforms and died in a second outbreak of violence in 121. The precedent mattered more than the laws: political disputes at Rome could now end in killing, and both sides had accepted it.

steps.name: Marius and the army
steps.page: Gaius Marius, consul seven times, beat Jugurtha in Africa and the Cimbri and Teutones in Italy, and in doing so opened the legions to citizens with no property. Men who owned no land served for pay and expected a farm at discharge, which only their commander could get them. The army's loyalty shifted from the state to the man who led it.

steps.name: The Social War and Sulla
steps.page: Rome's Italian allies revolted in 91 BCE over citizenship and won it by fighting. In the middle of that war Sulla, deprived of a command by a vote of the assembly, marched his legions on Rome, something no Roman had done. He returned from the east in 83 to do it again, made himself dictator, published proscription lists of enemies to be killed and their property sold, rewrote the constitution in the Senate's favour, and retired in 79.

steps.name: The First Triumvirate
steps.page: In 60 BCE Pompey, Crassus and Caesar agreed privately to pool their influence: Pompey wanted his eastern settlement ratified and land for his veterans, Crassus wanted favours for the tax farmers, Caesar wanted the consulship and a province. It was not an office and had no legal standing, and between them they controlled elections, legislation and commands for the next decade.

steps.name: Pharsalus and the dictatorship
steps.page: Pompey and most of the Senate abandoned Italy for Greece. Caesar beat them at Pharsalus in August 48 BCE; Pompey fled to Egypt and was murdered on arrival. Caesar spent the next three years destroying the remaining opposition in Egypt, Asia, Africa and Spain, and holding the dictatorship, from February 44 BCE for life.

steps.name: The Second Triumvirate and Philippi
steps.page: Antony, Octavian and Lepidus took formal joint power in 43 BCE and proscribed their enemies: some two thousand men, Cicero among them, were killed and their estates confiscated. In 42 BCE they destroyed the armies of Brutus and Cassius at Philippi in Macedonia; both killed themselves. The republican cause had no army left.

steps.name: The settlement of 27 BCE
steps.page: In January 27 BCE Octavian offered to give up his powers, and the Senate returned them with the name Augustus and a province containing most of the legions. A second settlement in 23 gave him the powers of a tribune for life and authority over other governors. He held no permanent office that was not republican, and he was answerable to no one.

name: Silk Road trade network
summary: Caravan routes linked China, Central Asia, Persia, India and the Mediterranean for some fifteen centuries.
body:
The Silk Road is the name given to the network of overland routes that linked China with Central Asia, Persia, India and the Mediterranean from about the second century BCE to the fifteenth century CE. Goods, people, ideas and disease moved along it, usually in relays rather than end to end.

The conventional starting point is the mission of Zhang Qian, sent west by the [Han](event:han-dynasty) court in 138 BCE to seek allies against the Xiongnu. He was held captive for years and came back with the first Chinese account of the states of Central Asia, and regular traffic followed. The routes ran from Chang'an through the Gansu corridor, split around the Taklamakan desert at its string of oasis towns (Dunhuang, Kashgar, Samarkand), and continued to Persia, the Levantine ports and, by sea, to India.

Very few merchants travelled the whole distance. Sogdian and later Arab and Persian traders worked stages of it, and a bolt of silk might change hands many times between China and Antioch. Silk went west, along with lacquer and later porcelain; horses, glass, wool, silver and gold came east. Ideas travelled as well: [Buddhism](event:spread-buddhism) travelled into China this way, [paper](event:paper-invention) travelled out, and Nestorian Christianity, Manichaeism and Islam all followed the same channels.

Traffic was safest under strong empires and worst in the gaps between them; the Mongol peace of the thirteenth century was its last great period. The [Black Death](event:black-death) almost certainly reached Europe along these routes. The wider network is treated in [the Silk Roads](item:silk-roads).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road).

name: The Silk Roads
summary: The overland and maritime routes that connected China, India, Persia and the Mediterranean, and the exchange of goods, technologies, religions and disease along them.
body:
The name is a nineteenth-century coinage for something that was never a single road. [The routes](item:silk-road) were a shifting web of caravan stages and sea lanes, worked in relays by merchants who rarely travelled their whole length; a bolt of silk might change hands twenty times between Chang'an and Antioch.

Goods moved in both directions (silk, porcelain and rhubarb west; horses, glass, silver and cotton east), and ideas moved with them. [Paper](item:paper-invention) reached Samarkand and then the Islamic world and Europe; [Buddhism](item:spread-buddhism) travelled from India into Central Asia and China; gunpowder, the compass and Indian numerals followed the same channels. The [Han](item:han-dynasty) mission of Zhang Qian in 130 BCE is the conventional starting point, and the *Pax Mongolica* under [Genghis Khan's](item:temujin-genghis-khan) successors its safest period, when [Marco Polo](item:marco-polo) made the journey.

Disease used the roads too: the [Black Death](item:black-death) almost certainly reached Europe along them. The overland trade declined as the Ming turned inward after [Zheng He](item:zheng-he-admiral) and as Portuguese ships opened a sea route to the Indies, but the maritime leg never stopped.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road).

name: Buddhism spreads along the Silk Road
summary: Buddhist monks and merchants carried the faith from India across Central Asia and into China.
body:
Part of [Life of the Buddha](event:buddha). [Buddhism](event:buddha) spread out of India into Central Asia and China along the [Silk Road](event:silk-road) in the last century BCE and the first centuries CE, carried by monks travelling with merchants and supported by the rulers of the states along the way.

[Ashoka's](event:maurya-empire) missions in the third century BCE had already taken it to Sri Lanka and the north-west. In Gandhara and Bactria, regions left Greek-speaking by [Alexander's](event:alexander-conquests) successors, it met Hellenistic sculpture, and the first images of the Buddha in human form were made there. The Kushan empire that ruled the region from the first century CE straddled the trade routes and patronised monasteries along them.

Chinese sources record Buddhist communities by the middle of the first century CE, and the Parthian monk An Shigao was translating texts at the Han capital of Luoyang by about 148. Translation was the central labour and took centuries: Indian terms had to be rendered into a language with an entirely different grammar and an existing philosophical vocabulary of its own, and the choices made shaped the religion that resulted.

Monasteries at the oasis towns served as hostels, banks and libraries as well as places of practice. The cave complexes at Dunhuang, Kizil and Bamiyan mark the road. From China the religion passed to Korea in the fourth century and to Japan in the sixth.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road_transmission_of_Buddhism).

name: Nazca geoglyphs constructed
summary: The Nazca people of Peru scratched enormous geometric and animal figures into the desert floor.
body:
The Nazca Lines are geoglyphs cut into the desert floor of the Nazca pampa in southern Peru. Several hundred are known: mostly straight lines, spirals and geometric figures, together with more than seventy outlines of animals and plants: a hummingbird, a monkey, a spider, a condor, a whale, a tree. They were made between about 500 BCE and 500 CE.

The technique is simple and the preservation is a matter of climate. The surface is covered in reddish-brown, iron-oxide-coated pebbles; removing them exposes pale yellow-grey ground beneath. The trenches are only 10 to 15 cm deep. Almost no rain falls, there is little wind at ground level, and the figures have survived two thousand years largely undisturbed. Wooden stakes found at the ends of lines suggest they were set out with cords and sighting posts, and the designs can be laid out accurately at full size from a small drawing by simple scaling.
