Their purpose is unresolved. Astronomical alignment, proposed as an explanation by Paul Kosok and pursued for decades by Maria Reiche, has not held up statistically for most of the lines. Current arguments favour ritual pathways walked in procession, connections with water sources and irrigation in a desert where water is the constraint, and figures meant to be seen by gods rather than by people.

Local inhabitants always knew of them; they were noticed from the air in 1940–41, when aircraft made the largest figures legible as wholes.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazca_Lines).

name: Julius Caesar
summary: Roman general and statesman whose conquest of Gaul, civil war and dictatorship ended the Republic in all but name.
body:
Caesar came from an old patrician family of no recent distinction. He built a career through popular politics and debt, and in 60 BCE joined Pompey and Crassus in the informal alliance later called the First Triumvirate, which secured him the consulship and then a long command in the north.

The [conquest of Gaul](item:caesar-gaul) between 58 and 50 BCE brought him wealth, a devoted army and a reputation his rivals could not match; his own account of it is still read. Ordered to give up his command, he [crossed the Rubicon](item:rubicon) in 49 BCE and took Italy in weeks. He defeated Pompey at Pharsalus, campaigned in Egypt, where he installed [Cleopatra](item:cleopatra-vii) on the throne, and returned to be made dictator, eventually for life.

He reformed the calendar, settled veterans in colonies across the Mediterranean and extended citizenship. On the Ides of March 44 BCE he was [assassinated](item:caesar-assassination) by a conspiracy of senators who hoped to restore the Republic. The wars that followed did the opposite, ending with his heir Octavian as [the first emperor](item:roman-republic-fall).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar).

name: Cleopatra VII
summary: The last ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt, who kept her kingdom independent for two decades by way of alliances with Rome's most powerful men.
body:
Cleopatra was a Macedonian Greek by descent, the last of the Ptolemies who had ruled [Egypt](item:alexandria) since the death of Alexander. She came to the throne at eighteen alongside a younger brother, was driven out, and returned with Roman backing after [Julius Caesar](item:julius-caesar) arrived in Alexandria in 48 BCE. She was reportedly the only member of her dynasty to learn Egyptian.

After Caesar's [assassination](item:caesar-assassination) she allied with Mark Antony, with whom she had three children and against whom Octavian turned Roman opinion. Their combined fleet was destroyed at [Actium](item:actium) in 31 BCE; both took their own lives the following year, and Egypt became a Roman province governed as the emperor's personal possession.

Her reign closed three thousand years of Egyptian monarchy. Almost everything written about her in antiquity comes from the side that defeated her, and the portrait of a seductress owes more to Augustan propaganda, and later to Shakespeare, than to the administrator the evidence suggests.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleopatra).

name: Caesar's conquest of Gaul
summary: Eight years of campaigning brought Gaul under Roman rule and gave Caesar the army with which he seized power.
body:
Part of [Fall of the Roman Republic](event:roman-republic-fall). Between 58 and 50 BCE Julius Caesar, as governor of the Gallic provinces, conquered the whole of Gaul, roughly modern France, Belgium and Switzerland with parts of the Netherlands and Germany. The campaigns made him the richest man in Rome and gave him an army that had served under him for eight years.

He began with a pretext: the migration of the Helvetii across Roman territory in 58 BCE, which he stopped, followed by a campaign against the German leader Ariovistus. He then went on to fight the Belgic tribes in the north, the maritime Veneti in Brittany, and Germanic groups across the Rhine, which he bridged twice as a demonstration. Two expeditions to Britain, in 55 and 54 BCE, achieved little militarily but were unprecedented and were reported to great effect at home.

A general revolt broke out in 52 BCE under Vercingetorix of the Arverni, who avoided battle and burned supplies. It ended at Alesia, where Caesar besieged the Gallic army behind one ring of fortifications while holding off a relief force with another. Vercingetorix surrendered and was executed in Rome six years later.

Caesar published his own account, the *Commentaries on the Gallic War*, in plain third-person Latin, and it is still read as a school text. Ancient writers put the dead at a million and the enslaved at another million; the figures cannot be checked, but the depopulation of parts of Gaul is not in doubt.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallic_Wars).

name: Caesar crosses the Rubicon
summary: Caesar led his army across the Rubicon into Italy proper, an act of war against the Senate that began the civil war.
body:
Part of [Fall of the Roman Republic](event:roman-republic-fall). In January 49 BCE Julius Caesar led a legion across the Rubicon, a small river marking the southern boundary of his province, into Italy. A general who entered Italy under arms forfeited his command by law, and the crossing began the civil war.

Caesar's command in Gaul was ending and the Senate, urged on by Pompey, required him to give up his army before standing for a second consulship. Disarmed, he could be prosecuted for the acts of his first consulship; his opponents said as much. He asked to keep his command until the election, was refused, and the Senate passed its emergency decree.

He crossed with the Thirteenth Legion. Suetonius reports that he quoted a line of Greek comedy ('let the die be cast'), which survives in Latin as *alea iacta est*. Town after town opened its gates, and within two months Pompey and most of the Senate had abandoned Italy for Greece, leaving Caesar in control of Rome without a battle fought in the peninsula.

The river itself cannot now be identified with certainty among the streams running into the Adriatic near Rimini. The phrase remains in use: crossing the Rubicon means passing a point from which there is no way back.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubicon).

name: Assassination of Julius Caesar
summary: A conspiracy of senators stabbed the dictator to death at a meeting of the Senate on the Ides of March, 44 BCE.
body:
Part of [Fall of the Roman Republic](event:roman-republic-fall). Julius Caesar was killed on 15 March 44 BCE at a meeting of the Senate held in the portico attached to the Theatre of Pompey. The conspirators, who called themselves the Liberators, numbered as many as sixty; the leaders were Marcus Junius Brutus and Gaius Cassius Longinus.

Caesar had been appointed dictator for life the month before, and had accumulated honours (a golden chair, statues among those of the kings, the right to wear triumphal dress) that looked to his opponents like preparation for a monarchy. He had also pardoned most of them, several of whom held office by his gift, and had dismissed his Spanish bodyguard.

He was surrounded as he sat, on the pretext of a petition, and stabbed. The physician Antistius is said to have found twenty-three wounds, only one of them fatal. The famous last words to Brutus come from Shakespeare by way of Suetonius, who reports the tradition and doubts it.

The conspirators had no plan beyond the killing. Antony's funeral oration turned the crowd against them, Caesar's will named his great-nephew Octavian as heir, and the two of them, with Lepidus, proscribed their opponents the following year. Brutus and Cassius were destroyed at Philippi in 42 BCE.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Julius_Caesar).

name: Battle of Actium
summary: Octavian's fleet defeated Antony and Cleopatra off western Greece; Egypt was annexed the following year.
body:
Part of [Fall of the Roman Republic](event:roman-republic-fall). The Battle of Actium was fought at sea on 2 September 31 BCE off the western coast of Greece, between the fleet of Octavian and the combined fleets of Mark Antony and [Cleopatra VII](item:cleopatra-vii) of Egypt. Octavian won, and was left the only military power in the Roman world.

The Second Triumvirate had divided the empire, Antony taking the east; his relationship with Cleopatra and his grants of Roman territory to their children gave Octavian the material for a propaganda campaign that presented the coming war as a defence of Rome against a foreign queen. War was declared on Egypt rather than on Antony.

Octavian's commander Marcus Agrippa cut Antony's supply lines and blockaded his fleet in the Ambracian Gulf through the summer. Antony broke out with part of it. In the fighting Cleopatra's squadron sailed through the gap with the war chest and Antony followed her; the ships left behind surrendered, and his land army capitulated within a week.

Octavian invaded Egypt the following year. Antony and Cleopatra both took their own lives in August 30 BCE, and Egypt was annexed, not as an ordinary province but as the emperor's own possession, with senators forbidden to enter it without permission. Its grain fed Rome for the next three centuries.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Actium).

name: Virgil composes the Aeneid
summary: Virgil's epic poem traced Rome's mythical origins and became the model of the heroic epic for two millennia.
body:
Virgil worked on the *Aeneid* from about 29 BCE until his death in 19 BCE. It is a Latin epic in twelve books of hexameter verse, tracing the Trojan Aeneas from the fall of Troy to Italy and the settlement from which Rome was to come.

The first half follows Homer's *Odyssey* (wandering, shipwreck, the year at Carthage with Dido and the descent to the underworld), and the second follows the *Iliad*, in a war in Latium against Turnus. Aeneas is defined by *pietas*, duty owed to gods, father and people, which requires him to abandon Dido and to fight a war he does not want. The poem is at once a foundation story for Rome and an account of what its founding cost, and readers have argued since antiquity about how far the second undercuts the first.

It was written under Augustus and connects his family to Aeneas and to Venus, with prophecies of Roman rule delivered in the underworld and on the shield of Aeneas. Virgil left it unfinished (a few lines are metrically incomplete) and is said to have asked that it be burned; Augustus overrode the request.

It became the central text of Roman education almost immediately, and stayed a school text through the Middle Ages. Dante made Virgil his guide through Hell and Purgatory.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid).

name: Founding of the Roman Empire
summary: The Senate granted Octavian the name Augustus and effective sole power, beginning two centuries of Roman peace.
body:
In January 27 BCE the Senate granted Octavian, sole victor of the civil wars, the name Augustus and a command over the provinces where most of the legions were stationed. The arrangement is conventionally taken as the founding of the Roman Empire, and it began two centuries of relative internal peace.

Augustus was careful never to hold a title that sounded like monarchy. He was *princeps*, first citizen; the Senate met, magistrates were elected, and the forms of the [Republic](event:roman-republic-fall) continued. What he actually held was control of the army, of the treasury of the provinces that paid for it, and of the succession. The system is called the principate.

The empire he left ran from Spain to Syria and from Britain (added in 43 CE) to the Sahara, holding perhaps fifty to sixty million people, a fifth or more of the world's population. It was governed with a small administration: local elites collected the taxes and ran the towns, and Roman citizenship, extended steadily and finally to nearly all free inhabitants in 212 CE, was the reward for cooperation. One currency, one body of [law](event:roman-law-growth), a professional standing army of some thirty legions and a network of [roads](event:roman-roads) held it together.

The *Pax Romana* ran to the [death of Marcus Aurelius](event:marcus-aurelius) in 180 CE. The empire survived crisis, division and [Christianisation](event:constantine), and its western half [ended in 476](event:rome-fall); the eastern continued from [Constantinople](event:constantinople-founded) for another thousand years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire).

name: Ovid writes the Metamorphoses
summary: Ovid's epic poem narrated myths of transformation and became one of the most widely read works of the ancient world.
body:
Ovid completed the *Metamorphoses* about 8 CE. It is a Latin poem in fifteen books and some twelve thousand lines of hexameter verse, retelling around 250 Greek and Roman myths, all of them involving a transformation of one thing into another.

The poem runs from the creation of the world out of chaos to the deification of Julius Caesar, and moves between stories by association rather than by plot: Daphne turning into a laurel to escape Apollo, Narcissus into a flower, Arachne into a spider, Pygmalion's statue into a woman, Midas and his touch, Orpheus and Eurydice, Philemon and Baucis. The transformations are frequently the outcome of violence or of divine caprice, and the poem parodies the epic form as often as it uses it.

Ovid was banished by Augustus to Tomis on the Black Sea in 8 CE, the year the poem was finished, for reasons he described only as 'a poem and a mistake'. He said he burned his own copy; others had already circulated.

It became the principal source of classical mythology for later Europe. Chaucer, Shakespeare, Milton and Dante drew on it, and it supplied subjects to painters and sculptors (Titian, Bernini, Rubens) more than any other ancient text.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metamorphoses).

name: Crucifixion of Jesus
summary: Jesus of Nazareth was executed in Roman Judaea; his followers' claim that he rose again founded Christianity.
body:
Jesus of Nazareth, a Jewish preacher from Galilee, was executed by crucifixion in Jerusalem under the Roman prefect Pontius Pilate, most probably in 30 or 33 CE. His followers' claim that he had risen from the dead is the origin of Christianity.

Crucifixion was a Roman penalty for slaves, rebels and provincials, designed to be slow and public. The gospels describe an arrest after a meal at Passover, a hearing before the Jewish authorities, a trial before Pilate on a charge that amounted to sedition, and execution outside the city walls between two others, with a placard naming him King of the Jews. That he was crucified under Pilate is one of the few points about him attested outside Christian writing: the Roman historian Tacitus mentions it, as does Josephus.

The movement that followed was at first one of several Jewish groups. Its decisive turn came with Paul of Tarsus, who preached to non-Jews and dropped the requirement of circumcision and the food laws, making the message portable across the Roman world. Written gospels followed in the decades after 70 CE.

Within three centuries the religion had [spread across the empire](event:spread-christianity) that executed him, and after [Constantine](event:constantine) it became the religion of the Roman state. Christianity is today the largest religion in the world, with over two billion adherents, and the Western calendar still counts its years from a sixth-century estimate of his birth.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crucifixion_of_Jesus).

name: Colosseum construction in Rome
summary: The Flavian Amphitheatre was built under emperors Vespasian and Titus, the largest such structure in the ancient world.
body:
Part of [Founding of the Roman Empire](event:roman-empire). The Colosseum, properly the Flavian Amphitheatre, was begun in Rome about 72 CE under Vespasian and inaugurated by his son Titus in 80 with a hundred days of games. It is the largest amphitheatre ever built.

The site was deliberate: it had been the ornamental lake of Nero's palace, and giving the ground back to the people as a public building was a statement about the new dynasty. The name came later, from a colossal statue of Nero that stood nearby.

The structure is an ellipse about 190 by 155 metres, four storeys high, built of travertine blocks, tuff and brick-faced [concrete](event:roman-concrete), with tiers of arches carrying engaged columns in the Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders. Estimates of capacity range from about 50,000 to 80,000 spectators. Eighty entrances and a system of numbered tickets and stairways let it be filled and emptied quickly, and seating was arranged strictly by rank. A retractable awning, worked by sailors, shaded part of the seating. Beneath the floor, a two-level basement of cells, corridors and lifts held animals and scenery.

It was used for gladiatorial combat, staged animal hunts and executions for some four centuries. It was later a fortress, a quarry and a Christian shrine; roughly two-thirds of the original fabric is gone, much of it into Renaissance Rome.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colosseum).

name: Pliny the Elder's Natural History
summary: Pliny compiled an encyclopedic survey of everything known about the natural world, minerals, animals and plants.
body:
Pliny the Elder published the *Natural History* about 77 CE and dedicated it to the future emperor Titus. It is an encyclopedia in thirty-seven books covering, in his own account, twenty thousand matters of note drawn from two thousand volumes by a hundred authors, and it is the model from which the later encyclopedic tradition descends.

The books run in order from cosmology and geography through anthropology, zoology, botany, agriculture and medicine to mineralogy, metals, painting, sculpture and precious stones. Pliny lists his sources book by book at the start, which is unusual for antiquity and makes the work a catalogue of lost literature as well as of things. He records folklore, marvels and error alongside careful observation and does not always distinguish them, but he is often the only surviving source. Most of what is known of Greek painters and of Roman techniques in mining, pigments and building comes from him.

He was a career official and cavalry officer who wrote in whatever hours he could take from his duties, and his nephew describes him being read to at meals and in the bath so as not to waste the time.

He died in the [eruption of Vesuvius](event:vesuvius) in 79 CE, commanding the fleet at Misenum, having taken ships across the bay both to observe the eruption and to take people off the shore.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_History_(Pliny)).

name: Eruption of Vesuvius destroys Pompeii
summary: An eruption of Mount Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and pyroclastic flow, preserving both.
body:
Part of [Founding of the Roman Empire](event:roman-empire). Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE and destroyed the Roman towns of Pompeii, Herculaneum, Oplontis and Stabiae on the Bay of Naples. The traditional date, 24 August, comes from the manuscripts of Pliny the Younger; charred inscriptions, autumn fruit and the clothing of the dead have led many scholars to prefer a date in October or November.

The eruption came in two stages. First a column of pumice and gas rose fifteen to thirty kilometres into the stratosphere and fell as ash and lapilli, mostly to the south-east, burying Pompeii metres deep and collapsing roofs under the weight. Then the column collapsed, sending pyroclastic surges (clouds of gas and debris at 200–300 °C) down the mountain. These reached Herculaneum first and killed everyone still there instantly, and later swept Pompeii.

The total death toll is unknown. Around 1,100 bodies have been recovered at Pompeii, where Giuseppe Fiorelli's technique of pouring plaster into the voids left in the ash gave casts of the dead in the positions they died in, and several hundred more were found in the boat sheds at Herculaneum in the 1980s.

Pliny the Younger watched from Misenum, about 30 km across the bay, and described the column and the panic in two letters to Tacitus written some twenty-five years later. They are the only eyewitness account, and eruptions of this kind are called Plinian after them.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eruption_of_Mount_Vesuvius_in_79_AD).

name: Teotihuacan
summary: A city of over 100,000 people in the Valley of Mexico, laid out along the Avenue of the Dead.
body:
Teotihuacan was a city in the Valley of Mexico, about 40 km north-east of the modern capital, which flourished from around 100 CE to 550. At its height it held between 100,000 and 200,000 people and was one of the largest cities in the world.

It was laid out on a grid, oriented about 15 degrees east of north, along a broad axis the Aztecs later called the Avenue of the Dead. The Pyramid of the Sun, some 65 metres high and one of the largest structures ever built in the Americas, stands on one side of it; the Pyramid of the Moon closes the northern end; and the Temple of the Feathered Serpent, in the walled compound at the southern end, was built over the graves of more than two hundred sacrificed people. Most of the population lived in single-storey walled apartment compounds, hundreds of them, plastered and painted with murals, an unusual arrangement for a Mesoamerican city.

Its inhabitants left no readable writing, and their language and ethnicity are unknown; distinct districts housed Zapotec and Gulf-coast groups, so it was plainly multi-ethnic. Its influence reached far: obsidian and pottery from Teotihuacan turn up across Mesoamerica, and in 378 CE a Teotihuacan-linked faction installed a new dynasty at [Tikal](event:maya-classic), 1,000 km away.

Around 550 the monuments along the central avenue were burned, apparently selectively; internal revolt is the usual explanation. The name is Nahuatl, given by the Aztecs to ruins already a thousand years old.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teotihuacan).

name: Moche civilisation of Peru
summary: The Moche of northern coastal Peru built irrigation canals, huge adobe platform mounds and finely modelled pottery.
body:
The Moche flourished on the desert coast of northern Peru from about 100 to 800 CE. They built irrigation systems, monumental adobe platforms and the most technically accomplished ceramics and metalwork in the pre-Columbian Andes.

They were not a single empire. The evidence points to a set of polities sharing a religion and an artistic style, divided at least between a northern and a southern group, each centred on a river valley running out of the Andes to the sea. Canals took water from these rivers across the desert between them and supported dense populations on ground that has no rainfall at all.

Their largest monuments are the Huaca del Sol and the Huaca de la Luna in the Moche valley, mounds of tens of millions of mould-made adobe bricks; the first is the largest adobe structure in the Americas. The Huaca de la Luna is painted with murals of a fanged deity and of prisoners led to sacrifice, and excavation there has found the remains of the sacrifices themselves, matching the scenes.

Moche potters made stirrup-spout vessels modelled as animals, plants, buildings, sexual acts and individual human faces so specific that they are usually described as portraits. The unlooted tomb of a ruler at Sipán, found in 1987, held gold, silver and turquoise regalia identical to that worn by figures in the painted ceremonies.

The culture declined from the sixth century, in a period of severe El Niño flooding alternating with prolonged drought.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moche_culture).

name: Rome supplied by eleven aqueducts
summary: A system of aqueducts brought water into Rome from as far as 90 km away, supplying baths, fountains and sewers on a scale no other ancient city matched.
body:
Part of [Founding of the Roman Empire](event:roman-empire). Rome was supplied with running water by a system of aqueducts built between 312 BCE and the third century CE. Nine were in service when Frontinus described them about 97 CE; two more were added later, giving the eleven the city is usually credited with.

The first, the Aqua Appia, was built underground in 312 BCE; the longest, the Aqua Marcia, ran about 91 km. Almost all of the length was in covered channels below ground, following the contour at a shallow, carefully surveyed gradient; the famous arcades carried the last stretch across the plain into the city, where the head of water was needed. Water ran continuously into distribution tanks and from them to public fountains, baths, and, for those who paid or who tapped the line illegally (which Frontinus complains about at length), private houses. The overflow flushed the sewers.

Estimates of the daily volume vary widely: figures derived from Frontinus have been read as up to a million cubic metres a day, while more conservative reconstructions give something between 520,000 and 635,000. Either way it is a quantity per head that European cities did not match again until the nineteenth century.

Some four hundred aqueducts were built across the empire, and their arcades at Segovia, Nîmes and elsewhere are among the most complete Roman structures standing.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqueduct_(Roman)).

name: Christianity spreads through the Roman Empire
summary: Three centuries after the crucifixion, Christianity had grown from a Judaean movement into a significant minority religion across the Mediterranean.
body:
Part of [Crucifixion of Jesus](event:crucifixion). In the three centuries after the [crucifixion](event:crucifixion), Christianity grew from a small Jewish movement in Judaea into a religion with communities in every province of the Roman Empire, numbering perhaps five to ten per cent of its population by 300 CE.

It spread along the same roads and sea lanes as trade, city by city, and was for a long time an urban religion. The Latin *paganus*, countryman, came to mean the opposite of Christian. Paul of Tarsus, writing in the 50s CE, had already made the decisive move of admitting non-Jews without requiring circumcision or the food laws. Congregations met in private houses under a local bishop; by the third century they held property, ran funds for widows and the poor, and corresponded across the Mediterranean in Greek and later Latin.

Historians usually explain its appeal by what it offered rather than by what it argued: membership open to anyone regardless of status or sex, an organised community that fed its poor and nursed its sick through epidemics, and a promise about death that the traditional cults did not make.

Persecution was intermittent rather than constant (under Nero in 64, then systematically under Decius in 250 and Diocletian from 303), and it produced a cult of martyrs that strengthened the communities it was meant to destroy. In 313 [Constantine](event:constantine) and Licinius ended it, and by 380 Christianity was the official religion of the empire.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Christianity).

name: Ancestral Puebloan civilization
summary: Farming peoples of the Four Corners built great houses, cliff dwellings and a road network, then left the region for the Rio Grande and the mesas of Arizona.
body:
The Ancestral Puebloans were the farming peoples of the Four Corners region, where the modern states of Utah, Colorado, Arizona and New Mexico meet. They grew maize, beans and squash on the Colorado Plateau, and are known for their masonry towns, their ceremonial architecture and the abrupt depopulation of their heartland in the thirteenth century.

Their culture is conventionally divided into Basketmaker and Pueblo periods. Pit houses gave way from about 750 CE to blocks of contiguous surface rooms built round sunken circular chambers, kivas, used for ceremony. The largest concentration was in Chaco Canyon in New Mexico, where between about 850 and 1150 they built great houses of core-and-veneer sandstone (Pueblo Bonito had over six hundred rooms and rose several storeys), with great kivas up to twenty metres across, aligned to solstices and lunar standstills, and dead-straight roads nine metres wide running for tens of kilometres across country that needed no roads for foot traffic. Turquoise, macaws and cacao found there came from as far as Mesoamerica.

Chaco was abandoned after a drought beginning about 1130. Population shifted north and west, and at Mesa Verde people built the cliff dwellings, set in alcoves under the canyon rims, that are the best known of all their sites, and left those too, within a century, during the long drought after 1276.

Their descendants are the Pueblo peoples of the Rio Grande, Acoma, Zuni and Hopi. The older name Anasazi is a Navajo word for enemy ancestors and is now generally avoided.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancestral_Puebloans).

name: Paper invented in China
summary: Cai Lun reported to the court a method of making sheets from plant fibres, cheap enough to replace bamboo and silk.
body:
Part of [Han dynasty](event:han-dynasty). In 105 CE the court official Cai Lun presented to the [Han](event:han-dynasty) emperor a method of making paper from tree bark, hemp waste, old rags and fishing nets. The report is the first clear description of the process, and it made paper cheap enough to displace everything else people wrote on.

Paper of a kind existed earlier (fragments used as wrapping survive from the second century BCE), but Cai Lun's contribution was a workable process with cheap raw materials: pulp the fibres, suspend them in water, lift a thin layer out on a screen, press and dry it. Before it, Chinese documents were written on strips of bamboo, which were heavy, or on silk, which was expensive; a memorial to the throne might arrive by cart.

The technique spread slowly. Korea and Japan had it by the seventh century. It reached the Islamic world in the eighth (tradition connects this to Chinese papermakers captured at the battle of Talas in 751), and mills at Samarkand and Baghdad supplied a book culture that grew with them. It entered Europe through Islamic Spain and Sicily, and paper mills were working in Italy by the thirteenth century.

Cheap writing material is a precondition for cheap books, and paper is what made [printing](event:printing) with movable type worth doing four centuries later.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_paper).

name: Roman Empire at its greatest extent
summary: Under Trajan the empire reached from Britain to Mesopotamia, ruling perhaps a fifth of humanity.
body:
Part of [Founding of the Roman Empire](event:roman-empire). The Roman Empire reached its greatest territorial extent in 117 CE, at the death of Trajan, covering roughly five million square kilometres from Britain to the Persian Gulf.

Trajan, who ruled from 98 to 117 CE, was the first emperor born outside Italy, in Spain. He fought two wars against the Dacian kingdom north of the Danube, in 101–102 and 105–106, annexed it as a province and brought back enough gold and silver to fund a building programme at Rome and 123 days of games. The campaigns are carved in a continuous spiral relief on the column that still stands in his forum. Arabia Petraea was annexed in 106. In 114 he attacked Parthia, took Armenia and Mesopotamia and reached the Persian Gulf.

The eastern conquests could not be held. Revolts broke out behind him, and his successor Hadrian gave up Mesopotamia and Armenia immediately on his accession in 117, fixing the frontier on the Euphrates and marking the northern limit in Britain with a wall.

The empire at this point ruled perhaps sixty to seventy million people, and later Romans regarded the reign as the high point: the Senate's formula for a new emperor was that he be luckier than Augustus and better than Trajan.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trajan).

name: Pantheon completed in Rome
summary: Hadrian built the most complete Roman temple still standing, with a vast dome and oculus open to the sky.
body:
Part of [Founding of the Roman Empire](event:roman-empire). The Pantheon in Rome was rebuilt under Hadrian and completed about 126 CE. It is the most complete building to survive from ancient Rome, and its dome remains the largest unreinforced [concrete](event:roman-concrete) dome in the world.

The inscription across the porch names Marcus Agrippa, who built the first temple on the site in 27–25 BCE; Hadrian kept the text when he replaced the burnt-out building entirely. What he built is two structures joined: a conventional Greek-style porch of granite columns, and behind it a domed cylinder unlike anything before it.

The interior is a perfect sphere, the dome's diameter and the height to its crown both about 43 metres. The concrete is graded from dense basalt aggregate at the base to light pumice at the top, the wall is hollowed out with relieving chambers, and the coffering lightens the shell further as it rises. The only light comes from an oculus nearly nine metres across, open to the weather, with the floor beneath it drained.

The building survived because it was given to the pope in 609 and consecrated as a church, which spared it the quarrying that took the rest of imperial Rome. Raphael is buried in it, as are two kings of Italy. Its dome was measured and copied by architects from Brunelleschi onwards.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantheon,_Rome).

name: Marcus Aurelius and the Meditations
summary: The last of the Five Good Emperors wrote personal philosophical meditations on Stoicism while ruling from 161 to 180 CE.
body:
Part of [Founding of the Roman Empire](event:roman-empire). Marcus Aurelius was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 CE and the last of the rulers later called the Five Good Emperors. He is remembered as much for the private notebook he kept, known as the *Meditations*, as for his reign.

He was adopted into the imperial family as a boy and educated in rhetoric and then in [Stoic](event:stoic-philosophy) philosophy, which he took seriously for the rest of his life. He ruled jointly with his adoptive brother Lucius Verus until Verus died in 169, the first time Rome had two emperors at once. The reign was almost entirely taken up with emergencies: a war with Parthia, the [Antonine Plague](event:antonine-plague) brought back by the returning armies, and the long Marcomannic Wars on the Danube, where Germanic and Sarmatian peoples broke into the provinces and reached northern Italy.

The *Meditations* were written in Greek, largely on campaign, and were not intended for publication. They contain no narrative and no politics: they are exercises in reminding himself that his position is temporary, that other people's faults follow from their ignorance, that pain and reputation are outside his control, and that duty is what remains.

He broke with his predecessors by leaving the throne to his own son, Commodus, who was assassinated in 192. Later writers treated Marcus as the nearest thing Rome had to Plato's philosopher-king.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Aurelius).

name: Antonine Plague
summary: An epidemic, probably smallpox, killed millions across the Roman world and thinned its armies.
body:
Part of [Founding of the Roman Empire](event:roman-empire). The Antonine Plague was an epidemic that spread through the Roman Empire between about 165 and 180 CE, with a further outbreak in 189. It is usually identified as smallpox, though measles has also been proposed and no case has been confirmed from remains.

It appeared first among the armies campaigning against Parthia in Mesopotamia and travelled back with them, reaching Rome by 166. The physician Galen, who lived through it, describes a fever with a black rash that dried into scabs and fell away after about nine days; the disease is sometimes called the Plague of Galen for that account.

Estimates of mortality are uncertain and disputed: figures of five to ten million dead, and death rates of perhaps a tenth of the population, are commonly cited, with much higher losses where people were crowded together in cities and in the army. The co-emperor Lucius Verus died in 169, possibly of it, and [Marcus Aurelius](event:marcus-aurelius) in 180 during a recurrence.

The consequences were structural. Recruitment was hard for years afterwards, campaigns on the Danube were interrupted, land went out of cultivation and prices and wages moved sharply. Historians disagree about how far the epidemic set the empire's later difficulties in motion, but it marks the end of the long expansion that preceded it.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonine_Plague).

name: Classic Maya civilisation
summary: Maya city-states in the lowlands built stepped pyramids, tracked the planets and kept the only fully developed writing system in the pre-Columbian Americas.
body:
The Classic period of Maya civilisation ran from about 250 to 900 CE across the lowlands of what is now Guatemala, Belize, southern Mexico and western Honduras. It was a landscape of competing city-states, each ruled by a dynasty that recorded its own history in stone.

There was never a single Maya state. Tikal, Calakmul, Copán, Palenque, Caracol and dozens of smaller centres fought, allied and intermarried, with Tikal and Calakmul heading rival networks for much of the period. Cities were built around plazas with stepped limestone pyramids, ball courts and palace compounds, and supported by intensive farming: terraces, raised fields in wetlands, and reservoirs that made settlement possible in country with no rivers and a long dry season.

The Maya writing system is the only fully developed script known in the pre-Columbian Americas: some eight hundred signs, mixing word signs and syllables, able to record the language exactly. Carved on stelae and lintels with [Long Count](event:maya-calendar) dates, the inscriptions name kings, their accessions, their wars and their rituals, the only dynastic history in the Americas that can be read directly. Most of it was deciphered only after the 1950s.

Between about 800 and 900 the southern cities stopped raising monuments and were abandoned, in a collapse now generally attributed to a combination of severe multi-decade drought, warfare and the failure of the political system that depended on kings delivering rain and victory. Cities in the northern Yucatán continued, and Maya peoples and languages are numerous today.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_civilization).

name: Kofun culture in Japan
summary: Japan's Kofun period saw the rise of a unified state, keyhole-shaped tombs, and early Chinese influence.
body:
The Kofun period, from about the middle of the third century to 538 CE, takes its name from the huge burial mounds (*kofun*) raised for the elite of early Japan. It is the period in which a central authority, the Yamato court, emerged in the Kinai region around modern Nara and Osaka.

The mounds are earthworks, often moated, and the largest have a distinctive keyhole shape (*zenpō-kōen-fun*, square at the front and round at the back), with the burial chamber under the round end. Many thousands survive. The largest, attributed by tradition to the emperor Nintoku, is about 486 metres long and covers more ground than any Egyptian pyramid; the imperial household administers many of these tombs and does not permit excavation. Their slopes were set with *haniwa*, unglazed clay cylinders and figures of warriors, horses, houses and servants.

Grave goods change over the period, from bronze mirrors and beads to iron armour, swords and horse harness, which points to a more militarised aristocracy and to close contact with the Korean peninsula. Immigrants and envoys from the Korean kingdom of Baekje brought technologies (sericulture, ironworking, irrigation) and, by tradition through the scholar Wani, Chinese writing, which was adopted for records at the Yamato court.

Buddhism arrived from Baekje in the sixth century, by tradition in 538 or 552, and its adoption marks the conventional end of the period. The chronicles compiled in the eighth century project a continuous imperial line back through it, which archaeology does not confirm.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofun_period).

name: Constantine legalises Christianity
summary: The Edict of Milan ended the persecution of Christians and set the empire on the path to a Christian state.
body:
Part of [Founding of the Roman Empire](event:roman-empire). In 313 CE the emperors Constantine and Licinius agreed at Milan to end the persecution of Christians, grant freedom of worship to everyone in the empire, and return confiscated church property. The agreement, usually called the Edict of Milan, is the point at which Christianity became a legal religion of the Roman state.

It followed the worst persecution the church had faced, begun by Diocletian in 303, and Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge outside Rome in 312, which he attributed to the Christian God after a vision reported in different forms by different writers.

Constantine went much further than toleration. He exempted clergy from public duties, funded church building at Rome and Jerusalem, gave bishops civil jurisdiction, and intervened directly in doctrinal disputes, summoning and presiding over the [Council of Nicaea](event:nicaea) in 325 to settle the question of Christ's relation to the Father. He [founded a new capital](event:constantinople-founded) at Byzantium, laid out with churches rather than temples. He was baptised only on his deathbed in 337, which was not unusual at the time.

Traditional cults were not banned and remained legal for most of the century. In 380 the Edict of Thessalonica made Nicene Christianity the official religion of the empire, and by the end of the century sacrifice had been prohibited. The church acquired wealth, hierarchy and imperial protection in the space of two generations.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Milan).

name: Gupta Empire
summary: A classical age of Indian art, literature and mathematics under the Gupta kings.
body:
The Gupta Empire ruled northern India from about 320 to 550 CE. Later writers treated it as a classical age, and much of what became standard in Indian art, literature, mathematics and temple architecture took shape under it.

It grew from a small kingdom in Magadha. Chandragupta I took the title of great king of kings about 320; his son Samudragupta campaigned from Bengal to the Deccan, and Chandragupta II, remembered as Vikramaditya, annexed the western satrapies and gave the empire access to the Arabian Sea ports. Government was looser than the [Mauryan](event:maurya-empire) model: defeated kings were often left in place as tributaries rather than replaced by governors.

Sanskrit was the language of the court and of a literature that includes Kalidasa's plays and poems, the *Shakuntala* above all. The Puranas took their present form, and the earliest surviving free-standing Hindu stone temples were built. The painted caves at Ajanta were largely completed in this period, and the seated Buddhas of Sarnath set the type copied across Asia. The Chinese pilgrim Faxian, who travelled in India around 400 CE, describes prosperous cities and free hospitals.

In mathematics and astronomy Aryabhata, writing in 499, gave a value of pi accurate to four decimal places, a sine table, and an explanation of day and night by the Earth's rotation. The [decimal place-value system](event:decimal-numerals) was in mature use.

Invasions by the Hunas from the late fifth century broke the empire's finances and its provinces, and it fragmented by about 550.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gupta_Empire).

name: First Council of Nicaea
summary: Bishops from across the empire agreed the Nicene Creed, defining orthodox Christian doctrine.
body:
Part of [Constantine legalises Christianity](event:constantine). The First Council of Nicaea met in 325 CE at Nicaea in Bithynia, summoned by the emperor Constantine. It was the first council to bring bishops from across the whole church together, and it produced the creed that still defines Christian orthodoxy.

The dispute that occasioned it came from Alexandria. Arius, a priest there, taught that the Son was created by the Father and had not existed eternally, that there was a time when he was not. His bishop condemned him; the argument spread through the eastern church and threatened the unity of an empire Constantine had just reunified by force.

Some 250 to 300 bishops attended, at imperial expense. They condemned Arius and adopted a statement of faith describing the Son as begotten, not made, and *homoousios* (of the same substance) with the Father, a term found nowhere in scripture and chosen because the Arians could not accept it. All but two bishops signed. The council also fixed the calculation of Easter independently of the Jewish calendar, settled the standing of clergy who had lapsed under persecution, and issued twenty canons of church discipline.

It did not end the controversy: Arian and semi-Arian parties held the upper hand for much of the next fifty years, and several of the Germanic peoples who entered the empire were converted by Arian missionaries. The creed was revised and extended at Constantinople in 381, and it is that version which is recited today.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Council_of_Nicaea).

name: Foundation of Constantinople
summary: Constantine refounded Byzantium as a new imperial capital, which remained a capital for sixteen centuries.
body:
Part of [Constantine legalises Christianity](event:constantine). Constantine refounded the Greek city of Byzantium as a new imperial capital and dedicated it on 11 May 330 CE. Constantinople (now Istanbul) remained a capital for sixteen centuries.

The site is the reason. It stands on a peninsula between the Sea of Marmara and the deep natural harbour of the Golden Horn, commanding the straits between the Mediterranean and the Black Sea and the land route between Europe and Asia. Water protects it on three sides, so a single wall across the landward approach defends the whole city; the walls Theodosius II built in 413, a triple line with a moat, were not breached by an enemy army for a thousand years.

Constantine laid out a forum, a hippodrome and a senate house, and stripped monuments from cities across the empire to furnish them. Grain from Egypt was redirected to feed it. Unlike Rome, it was Christian from the start, and it became the seat of a patriarch whose rivalry with the pope ran through the whole medieval period.

When the western empire [ended in 476](event:rome-fall), the eastern half went on being governed from here as the Roman Empire. The name Byzantine is a modern label its inhabitants never used. The city fell to the Fourth Crusade in 1204 and, finally, to the [Ottomans](event:fall-constantinople) in 1453.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinople).

name: Migration Period
summary: Two centuries of movement by Gothic, Vandal, Frankish, Hunnic and Lombard peoples into the Roman provinces remade the map of Europe.
body:
The Migration Period is the name given to the movement of peoples into and across the Roman Empire between roughly 375 and 568 CE, at the end of which the western provinces had become a set of Germanic kingdoms. German historiography calls it the *Völkerwanderung*, the wandering of the peoples.

The groups involved were not the sealed nations of nineteenth-century histories. Modern work treats them as coalitions that formed and re-formed around successful leaders and could absorb anyone who joined (Goths, Vandals, Suebi, Alans, Franks, Burgundians, Lombards), and much of the movement was of armies with their families rather than of whole populations. Many had served Rome as federate troops for generations before they took provinces of their own.

Nor was it simply invasion. The western empire kept losing the tax base that paid its army, so it hired the newcomers, settled them on land, and gave their leaders Roman titles; each such settlement made the next one harder to refuse. By the mid-fifth century the imperial government in Ravenna controlled little outside Italy, and the field armies were commanded by men of Germanic origin.

What emerged were the successor kingdoms: Visigothic Spain, Vandal Africa, Frankish Gaul, Ostrogothic and then Lombard Italy, Anglo-Saxon Britain. They kept Roman law and administration where they could and converted to Catholic Christianity within a few generations. Whether the period is best described as collapse or as transformation has been argued for two hundred years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migration_Period).

steps.name: The Huns enter Europe
steps.page: A mounted people from the steppe crossed the Volga in the 370s, destroyed the Alan confederation and broke the Gothic kingdom north of the Black Sea. Nothing about their origin is certain, and the identification with the Xiongnu of Chinese sources is argued both ways. What is clear is the pressure they put on everyone west of them.

steps.name: The Goths cross the Danube
steps.page: In 376 large numbers of Goths asked to be admitted to the empire as refugees and were let across the Danube. Roman officials extorted and starved them until they revolted. At Adrianople in August 378 the eastern emperor Valens attacked without waiting for reinforcements and was killed with much of his army, the worst Roman defeat in centuries and the first time a barbarian force had destroyed a field army inside the empire.

steps.name: The Rhine crossing
steps.page: On the last day of 406, or perhaps a year earlier, a large group of Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed the Rhine near Mainz and moved into Gaul, which the empire never fully recovered. Britain was left to itself at about the same time. Within three years the same groups had crossed the Pyrenees into Spain.

steps.name: The Vandals take Carthage
steps.page: The Vandals crossed from Spain to Africa in 429 and took Carthage ten years later, seizing the richest province of the west and the grain supply of Rome with it. They built a fleet, raided the Mediterranean at will, and sacked Rome themselves in 455. Roman and eastern attempts to recover Africa failed until Justinian's expedition of 533.

steps.name: Attila in Gaul and Italy
steps.page: Attila united the Hunnic confederation and extracted tribute from Constantinople before turning west. In 451 he invaded Gaul and was checked at the Catalaunian Plains by a Roman and Visigothic army under Aetius; the following year he ravaged northern Italy and withdrew. He died in 453, and his empire fell apart within two years.

steps.name: The last western emperor
steps.page: In 476 the commander Odoacer deposed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna and, rather than appoint a successor, sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople and ruled Italy as king. Contemporaries barely remarked on it (the west had been governed by generals for decades), but it is the conventional date for the [end of the western empire](event:rome-fall).

steps.name: The Lombards enter Italy
steps.page: Italy had just been reconquered for the eastern empire by Justinian, in twenty years of war that ruined it. In 568 the Lombards moved down from Pannonia and took most of the north and much of the interior, leaving the empire the coasts and Ravenna. Their arrival is the usual end point of the Migration Period.

name: Jerome translates the Bible into Latin
summary: Jerome produced the Vulgate, a Latin translation from Hebrew and Greek that became the Church's standard scripture for 1,200 years.
body:
Jerome produced the Latin Bible known as the Vulgate between 382 and 405 CE. It was the standard scripture of western Christianity for more than a thousand years.

Pope Damasus I commissioned him in 382 to sort out the Latin gospels, which circulated in many divergent translations from the Greek. Jerome revised them, moved to Bethlehem in 386, learned Hebrew, and translated the Old Testament from the Hebrew rather than from the Greek Septuagint that the church had used since its beginning. He called the principle *hebraica veritas*, the Hebrew truth. Augustine objected that changing familiar readings would unsettle congregations, and in some places it did.

The result is not one uniform work (the Psalms circulated in more than one of his versions, and some books he left in the older Latin), but it was accurate, readable, and gradually displaced everything else. It was in general use by the seventh century and was the text from which medieval Europe learned scripture, argued theology and drew a large part of its vocabulary: *creatura*, *salvatio*, *iustificatio*.

It was the first substantial book printed by Gutenberg. The Council of Trent declared it authentic in 1546 in response to Protestant translations from the Greek and Hebrew, and a corrected edition of 1592 remained the Catholic Church's official text until the twentieth century.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgate).

name: Visigoths sack Rome
summary: Alaric's Goths took the city for the first time in eight hundred years, shocking the Roman world.
body:
Part of [Migration Period](event:migration-period). On 24 August 410 CE the Visigoths under Alaric entered Rome and plundered it for three days. It was the first time a foreign army had taken the city in eight hundred years.

Alaric was not an outsider to the empire. He had commanded Gothic troops in Roman service, held the rank of *magister militum*, and had spent years trying to obtain land for his people and a regular supply of grain. He besieged Rome three times while negotiating with the imperial court at Ravenna, which repeatedly refused terms; on the third occasion the Salarian Gate was opened, whether by treachery or by a slave revolt.

The sack was moderate by the standards of ancient warfare. Christian writers record that the basilicas of St Peter and St Paul were treated as sanctuaries and spared, and that many inhabitants were ransomed rather than killed, though a great deal was looted and buildings were burned. Alaric died within months, before he could cross to Africa.

The military consequences were slight (Ravenna had been the capital for a decade, and the empire lost no territory), but the shock was enormous. Jerome, in Bethlehem, wrote that the whole world had perished in one city; the accusation that abandoning the old gods had brought it about prompted Augustine to begin *The City of God*.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(410)).

name: Decimal place-value system and zero
summary: Indian mathematicians formalised positional decimal notation with zero as a number in its own right.
body:
The decimal place-value system (ten digits in which position determines value, and a zero that both holds an empty place and works as a number) took its mature form in India between the fifth and seventh centuries CE. It is the notation the whole world now calculates in.

The digits descend from the Brahmi numerals, which had separate signs for units, tens and hundreds. The decisive step was writing only the units and letting position do the rest, which requires a symbol for an empty column. The Sanskrit *Lokavibhaga* of 458 CE uses place value with a word for zero; Aryabhata's astronomy of 499 assumes the system; and the Bakhshali manuscript, whose dating is disputed, has a dot for it.

Brahmagupta, writing the *Brahmasphutasiddhanta* in 628, gave the first known rules for arithmetic with zero and with negative quantities: what happens when zero is added to, subtracted from or multiplied by a number, and that debts and fortunes multiply in the way positive and negative numbers do. He did not give a consistent rule for division by zero.

Indian astronomical works reached Baghdad in the eighth century, and [al-Khwarizmi's](event:al-khwarizmi) treatise on calculating with Hindu numerals carried the system into Arabic. It entered Europe through Latin translations of that work and through Fibonacci's *Liber Abaci* of 1202, and displaced Roman numerals over the following three centuries. Written calculation, as opposed to counting on an abacus, depends on it entirely.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu–Arabic_numeral_system).

name: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
summary: The last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed at Ravenna, ending Roman rule in the west.
body:
In 476 CE the commander Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus, the last emperor to rule in Italy, and did not replace him. The date is conventionally given as the end of the Western Roman Empire, though nothing much happened on it and contemporaries did not treat it as an ending.

The decline was long and had many causes, and historians have never agreed on their weight. Recurring civil wars and short reigns; the loss of Africa, Spain and Gaul to the peoples of the [migration period](event:migration-period), and with them the tax revenue that paid the army; a currency debased and an administration that could no longer collect; armies increasingly recruited from outside the empire and commanded by men whose loyalty was personal; plague and a colder, drier climate. The [sack of Rome in 410](event:rome-sack-410) and again in 455 showed how little was left to defend it.

By the 470s the western emperor governed little beyond Italy, and real power lay with his generals. Odoacer sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople and asked to rule Italy as a patrician under the eastern emperor. The legal fiction of a single empire continued.

The western provinces became the Germanic successor kingdoms, in which Roman law, Latin and the church survived while the tax state and the standing army did not. The eastern half, ruled from [Constantinople](event:constantinople-founded), was not affected and lasted until 1453. 'The fall of Rome' is therefore a statement about the west, and about a process rather than a year.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire).
